Response-2: We fully agree with the reviewer that dexamethasone exhibits potent anti-
inflammatory properties and is widely used as an anti-inflammatory agent in various clinical
settings. However, it is important to emphasize that these effects generally manifest after
prolonged corticosteroid treatment. In our studies, dexamethasone was used solely as a
neutrophil demarginating agent in conjunction with NE as an experimental tool. Our data is
consistent with data from a recent study in humans that showed successful application of both
DEX and NE as demarginating agents (PMID: 26858400) to elucidate the mechanisms of
neutrophil demargination.
point that interactions between neutrophils and macrophages, DCs, and T cells cannot be ruled
out. However, TBI is primarily used in our models to deplete stem cells to completely halt
granulopoiesis. Despite the absence of routine granulopoiesis, both MI induction and DEX
administration were still able to increase circulating neutrophil numbers, suggesting that
marginated (matured cells that were not killed by TBI) neutrophils serve as the primary source
of neutrophils in the heart immediately after MI. While it remains challenging to determine
whether this increase results from interactions between neutrophils and other immune cells, our
study primarily aimed to identify the sources of neutrophils post-MI. That said, we cannot
completely exclude the involvement of other cytokines in neutrophil demargination during DEX
and NE treatment. As suggested by the reviewer, we conducted a cytokine array to evaluate
systemic inflammatory markers following DEX/ NE treatment. The resulting data are presented
in Table 1. As shown in the Table 1, DEX/NE treatment for 6 hours has no significant impact on
any of the major cytokines tested. We also present serum cytokine data (Table -2) in sham and
MI mice at different time points post-MI to show how MI increase certain inflammatory cytokines
as early as 6 hours but not DEX or NE.
Comment-3. Please also consider discussing whether the observed demargination is a
localized response (specific to ischemic tissue) or part of a systemic phenomenon. To gain a
more comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms underlying neutrophil demargination in
MI, it would be beneficial to explore the interplay between β-AR signaling and other relevant
pathways, such as those mediated by chemokines and adhesion molecules. Additionally,
considering the long-term consequences of excessive neutrophil recruitment, such as impaired
tissue repair and adverse cardiac remodeling, would provide valuable insights into the clinical
implications of the authors findings.
Response-3: This is an important point. As suggested, we have included this in our discussion
under the limitations (Page 20). We believe that neutrophil demargination represents a systemic
response driven by sympathetic nervous system (SNS) activation. However, it is likely triggered
by ischemic damage (i.e., MI) to the heart, as sham surgeries—while likely activating the SNS
to some extent—did not cause a similar neutrophil demargination response.
The interplay between β-AR signaling and those mediated by chemokines and adhesion
molecules is indeed complex, and defining this interplay in detail is beyond the scope of this
study. Indeed, it is well established that chemokines and cytokines activate the endothelium,
promoting the adhesion of leukocytes to the vessel wall. In contrast, β-adrenergic receptor (β-
AR) stimulation on neutrophils promotes their migration away from the endothelium by
suppressing the expression of adhesion molecules. This facilitates neutrophil movement into
both the circulation and the affected tissues. The delicate balance between adhesion and
migration is critical for regulating neutrophil trafficking during inflammatory responses and
ensuring proper immune responses without excessive tissue damage.
Regarding the long-term consequences of neutrophil recruitment, previous studies, including
our own, have shown that excessive neutrophil infiltration into the heart can exacerbate infarct
expansion and impair cardiac remodeling (PMID:31941367). On the other hand, indiscriminate
depletion of neutrophils beyond the inflammatory phase post-MI (after day 3) may negatively
affect wound healing. The findings presented in this manuscript are particularly significant, as
they identify β2 ARs as a promising therapeutic target to modulate excessive neutrophil
recruitment to the heart, particularly in the critical early hours following MI.
Comment-4. To directly measure β2-AR activation in neutrophils, phospho-specific antibodies
(to measure phosphorylated proteins downstream of the receptor, e.g., p-ERK1/2, p-Akt, p-p38
MAPK) should be employed in isolated neutrophils stimulated with a β2-adrenergic agonist like
2
isoproterenol or inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and CXCL8) to
mimic the inflammatory response. This could provide further evidence for the role of β2-ARs in
mediating neutrophil demargination.
Response: This is an important consideration, as neutrophils express a range of cytokine
receptors that could influence their behavior during demargination. To explore this, we
conducted immunoblotting studies using representative ligands: isoproterenol (a β-adrenergic
receptor agonist), TNF-α (a pro-inflammatory cytokine), and CXCL1 (a chemokine that signals
through CXCR1 and CXCR2). Notably, mice do not express CXCL8; instead, they produce
GCP-2/LIX, which also signals via CXCR1/2. Therefore, we used CXCL1 to mimic relevant
chemokine signaling. As shown in Figure-R1, stimulation of bone marrow neutrophils with these
ligands for 6 hours did not induce activation of ERK, AKT, or p38 MAPK pathways. In fact,
phosphorylation of some signaling proteins (e.g., P-AKT) was reduced following treatment with
TNF-α, CXCL1, or isoproterenol. These results suggest that MAPK pathways are unlikely to
mediate neutrophil demargination in response to cytokine or β2-adrenergic receptor activation.
This conclusion is further supported by our proteomics data (Supplemental Figure 2), which
showed no enrichment of MAPK pathway activation despite general GPCR engagement.
Instead, we observed significant changes in proteins involved in actin polymerization and
cytoskeletal remodeling, particularly through calcium-regulated pathways. These included Rac,
Pak, Rho, as well as key regulators of cell polarity and motility such as ROCK, Cofilin (CFN),
Profilin, and LIM kinase (LIMK). Collectively, these findings support a model in which β2-AR-
and cytokine-driven neutrophil demargination is primarily mediated through cytoskeletal and
calcium-dependent signaling rather than MAPK activation.
Comment-5. To complement the proteomics analysis of demarginated neutrophils post- MI or
NE administration, which revealed the activation of processes involved in cellular movement
and cytoskeletal reorganization, visualizing changes in cellular morphology and cytoskeletal
reorganization would provide additional insights. Immunofluorescence microscopy should be
used to show changes in cell shape, formation of pseudopodia, and cytoskeletal dynamics in
response to β-AR activation.
Response-5: Previous studies (PMID: 26858400) have demonstrated that cytoskeletal
reorganization—specifically changes in F-actin intensity and its localization—can reliably
indicate neutrophil motility in response to DEX or NE stimulation. While we acknowledge the
reviewer’s suggestion to include additional markers, we believe that incorporating them would
not significantly change the primary conclusions of our study. Nonetheless, to address this
feedback, we performed additional immunofluorescence staining on mouse blood cells treated
ex vivo with either PBS or NE for 6 hours. As shown in Figure-R2, NE stimulation led to a
pronounced spreading of F-actin and the formation of pseudopodia, consistent with cytoskeletal
remodeling. These findings support the conclusion that β-adrenergic receptor (β-AR) activation
by NE promotes cytoskeletal reorganization, a hallmark of neutrophil motility and migration.
Comment-6: Figure 5 j,k and Figure 6 h,i: Please check your scale bars! From my point of view,
magnifications are not the same, so the scale bars cannot be the same size!
Response: Thank you for bringing this to our attention. We have now corrected the error and
included the appropriate scale bar.
Comment-1: In this paper the authors propose that neutrophil demargination induced by NE via
beta-2 adrenergic receptors, rather than neutrophil production and mobilization from the BM or
spleen, is responsible for the first wave of neutrophil infiltration in the heart after myocardial
infarction in mice. Figure 1 examines kinetics of granulopoiesis and granulocyte dynamics in
various compartments i.e. BM blood spleen heart, showing that peak heart infiltration occurs
before peak granulopoiesis suggesting non-BM/spleen source of neutrophils for early
recruitment. Figure 2 uses a model of total body irradiation to disrupt granulopoiesis, and treat
mice with demargination inducing agents (DEX, NE), providing data supporting the notion that
demarginating neutrophils are recruited to the heart early after MI. In Figure 3 the authors
performed proteomics analysis of blood neutrophil 6 hours after MI or NE and NE+propranolol
treatment. Figure 4/5: the authors use various treatments to prevent NE synthesis of block
different beta adrenergic receptors (Fig 4) or use mice with myeloid specific deficiency in beta2
or beta1+beta2 AR (Fig 5), proposing a role of beta2-AR in neutrophil demargination and
recruitment to the heart after MI. Figure 6 shows that short term, but not long term, propranolol
treatment improves cardiac repair after permanent MI in mice.
The paper is clearly written, the proposed conclusions are an important and a new contribution
to the field. There are however several technical and conceptual issues, including insufficiently
powered experiments and unexpected results in the LAD permanent ligation model. I would
furthermore suggest toning down the conclusions as most evidence is indirect and discuss the
weaknesses and limitation of the different experimental approaches in more details.
Response-1: We appreciate the constructive feedback and thank you for your suggestion. We
have repeated most of the previously underpowered experiments and have included new
figures. Additionally, we have addressed the limitations of the LAD model and have refined our
conclusions accordingly.
Comment-2: One weakness of the paper is that it is technically not possible to clearly
distinguish neutrophil origin and most of the provided evidence is indirect. Thus, most of the
conclusion are overstated e.g. line 155 “Since we found no role for either BM or spleen”. While
experiments such as those presented in Figure 1 are informative, they only provide indirect
evidence as the different compartments observed are not merely ‘communicating vases’, and
the number of neutrophils at a given time point in the BM represents a complex balance
between production, retention, mobilization and reverse-migration. The EdU experiments show
neutrophils originating from HSPCs that have proliferated during the labeling period, but mature
neutrophils originating from BM or spleen reservoirs and mobilized early after MI cannot be
distinguished from demarginating neutrophils. However, the cumulative amount of evidence
provided by the authors indeed suggests that demargination is a substantial source of early
neutrophil recruitment to the heart.
Response-2: We completely agree with the reviewer. Delineating the various mechanisms by
which neutrophils are sourced from different compartments and recruited to the heart post-MI is
indeed challenging. As the reviewer correctly pointed out, the number of neutrophils in
circulation at any given time reflects a delicate balance between their production, mobilization,
retention, and elimination.
Notably, our total body irradiation (TBI) studies provide crucial evidence that mature neutrophils
(protected from radiation) are mobilized from the vasculature during bone marrow ablation. We
appreciate the reviewer’s recognition that our findings support the notion that demargination is a
significant source of early neutrophil recruitment to the heart.
Comment-3: Figure 1A-B: please show pre-gating strategy. There is possibly an error in
percentages showed as they are exactly the same between heart and blood
blood and heart have now been included. Additionally, we have provided the gating strategy for
the data in figures1A and B (Figure. R3).
Comment-4: -The authors conclude that neutrophil numbers are not affected in the BM at 6
hours, but the data shown in Figure 1E is not very robust, the experiment being insufficiently
powered with clear outlier observations.
Response-4: A slight reduction in neutrophil numbers was observed at 6 hours post-myocardial
infarction (MI) compared to the Sham group; however, this difference was not statistically
significant. We repeated the experiment, and similar results were obtained (Figure 1E).
Importantly, inclusion of these additional data points did not alter the overall statistical outcome.
Comment-5: Line 182: “wherein the blood neutrophil count is slightly decreased”. According to
Figure S1D the neutrophil count might be close to 0 at 18h, but there is actually no
measurement performed at this time point
Response: That is correct. Both neutrophil and total WBC counts drastically decrease following
bone marrow ablation. Please note that since we were able to completely deplete neutrophils by
12 hours, we did not measure them again to avoid causing unnecessary stress to the irradiated
animals. Additionally, the 18-hour time point was selected carefully after several preliminary
studies to identify a time when neutrophils are completely depleted without resulting in mortality
in the mice.
Comment-6: Neutrophil counts in the bone marrow and spleen should be provided for all
interventions.
Response-6: Thank you for the suggestion. We do have data on neutrophil counts in both the
bone marrow and spleen for all treatments. These results have now been included in Figure-R4
for completeness.
Comment-7: Many experiments are quite underpowered with sometimes as few as n=3 for
functional readouts in a model known for its quite substantial variability. Interexperiment
variability also seems quite high with e.g. a very wide range of reported blood neutrophil counts
in the control groups across experiments.
Response-7: Yes, some of our initial histological analyses were underpowered due to
unanticipated loss of animals during surgery, which prevented us from reaching the originally
planned group sizes. To address this, we have repeated the experiments and included
additional animals in the previously underpowered groups to strengthen the robustness and
reliability of the results. Please see figures 1, 2, 4, 5L-M, 6J-K and supplementary figures S1H,
S1I, S5I and S5J with new statistical analysis.
Comment-8: Figure 6B shows a 90% death rate in the control MI group, this is rather unusual
in this model. The effect of short-term propranolol treatment with almost no scar formation after
LAD ligation (Figure 6H-K) also does not seem very realistic, this would represent a spectacular
cardioprotective effect in this permanent ischemia model. Whether and how blinding and
randomization were performed is not indicated in the methods.
Response-8: Please note that Figure 6B shows 70% mortality (not 90%) in the control MI
group. This is quite typical, as the untreated mice experience extensive ventricular damage,
such as thinning and rupture. Additionally, our MI surgeries resulted in a large infarct size.
Regarding the short-term propranolol treatment, these data are not entirely surprising, as
neutrophils are the first cells to arrive at the infarct site, and their presence influences the
subsequent inflammatory response. This leads to the secretion of various proteases, which in
turn contribute to cardiac tissue damage. We believe that by preventing excessive neutrophil
5
infiltration, we could reduce the extent of damage to the heart. Please note that these mice were
administered a dose of propranolol 8 hours prior to MI induction as part of a preemptive
strategy. Regarding blinding and randomization, the IHC data were performed by a technician
(Nitin), while surgeries were conducted by Dr. Park, and drugs were injected by Dr. Dahdah.
Although Dr. Dahdah was aware of the group assignments and drugs, the technician was
blinded to the group allocations.
Comment-9: The methods do not mention the use of analgesics prior to or after MI surgery.
Response-9: We apologize for any oversight. We used a long-acting analgesic
(Buprenorphine) for all our MI surgeries, and this information has now been included in the
methods section. Please see supplemental file page 3.
Comment-10: Previous work showing splenic retention of immune cells in mice with myeloid
beta2-AR deficiency early (24 hours) after MI suggests that some of the effects observed here
might also be caused by splenic or medullar retention of neutrophils.
Response-10: While we acknowledge previous studies reporting splenic retention of immune
cells in mice with myeloid β2-AR deficiency early after MI, it is unclear whether this mechanism
is relevant to our model. We quantified neutrophil numbers in both the BM and spleen of β2⁻/⁻
and DKO mice at 6 hours and 30 days post-MI. As shown in Figure R5, there were no
statistically significant differences at either time point. These findings suggest that neutrophil
retention in these reservoirs does not account for the reduced neutrophil numbers observed in
the heart or blood post-MI in β2 BMT mice. This interpretation is further supported by prior data
showing that NE injections do not mobilize neutrophils from the BM or spleen under steady-
state conditions, indicating that the absence of β2-ARs does not result in abnormal retention in
these tissues, at least in the short term.
Comment-11: Assessment of neutrophil purity after magnetic sorting for proteomics studies is
missing
Response: Before subjecting neutrophils to any downstream applications, including
proteomics, we always conduct a quick flow cytometry analysis to confirm their purity. This data
has now been included in the proteomics figure 3B.
Comment-12: Full list of differentially abundant proteins to provide as supplementary table,
here only unannotated heatmap + pathway analyses are shown. It would be a good addition to
provide some cross-validation of proteomics and flow cytometry data e.g. do the authors see
downregulation of CD62L in the proteomics data and can some up/down proteins identified by
proteomics be validated by flow?
Response-12: We have included the complete list of proteins identified in our proteomics
analysis in the supplementary table; please refer to Sheet 1 labeled “Proteins” for relative
abundance data. CD62L was not detected, likely due to its well-documented shedding upon
neutrophil activation following MI. As a surface protein, CD62L is rapidly cleaved and released
into the extracellular space, and since our proteomics analysis was performed on cell pellets—
which exclude shed or secreted proteins—it was likely not captured. Similarly, several other
surface proteins were also absent from our dataset for this reason.
Comment-13: -Lines 307-308: ‘Administration of NE resulted in the activation of an immune
response that was very similar to that induced by MI’ : how was this formally quantified?
Overlap of up/down proteins induced by MI or NE?
Response-13: This conclusion was based on the observation that both MI and NE similarly
influenced pathways related to immune cell movement and trafficking, with comparable pathway
activation scores (MI: 22.6; NE: 24.7). However, we acknowledge that the original wording may
6
have overstated the similarity. We have revised the sentence to more accurately reflect the data
and clarify that while there is a comparable impact on specific pathways, we did not formally
quantify the overlap of individual upregulated or downregulated proteins between the MI and NE
groups.
Reviewer #3
Comment -1: A major limitation of the study is the use of the permanent ligation of the LAD to
induce myocardial infarction in mice, a species devoid of collateral coronary circulation (which in
contrast is abundantly present in the canine model). Full LAD ligation will prevent influx of
inflammatory cells (neutrophils and monocytes) in the infarcted area in the first few hours after
ligation, despite the statements to the contrary by the authors. They do not provide any
histological data at 6h post MI that would corroborate the presumed influx of neutrophils in the
infarct territory. The FACS data, listed in figure 1 to underpin their claim, do not provide the
required scientific evidence to substantiate this critical statement, as the data are derived from
whole LV homogenates. The authors need to provide histological sections prepared at 6h post
MI and stain for the presence of infiltrating neutrophils. They should next (semi)quantitate the
degree of trafficking in their subsequent studies with different pharmacological and genetic
interventions.
Response-1: We recognize that the LAD ligation model does not fully replicate the clinical
presentation of human acute coronary syndrome (ACS). However, our study design was
informed by recently published guidelines for in vivo murine models of myocardial infarction
(PMID: 34623181; PMID: 34114891), which provide standardized recommendations for both
reperfused and non-reperfused MI models. These guidelines outline key benchmarks for
evaluating left ventricular (LV) remodeling and function post-MI and support the use of the non-
reperfused LAD ligation model as the preferred approach for mechanistic studies of post-MI
inflammation.
To further address this limitation, we performed additional studies using an ischemia-
reperfusion injury (IRI) model to assess early neutrophil infiltration into the heart at 6 hours post-
injury. We also investigated the effects of short-term β-adrenergic blockade with propranolol on
neutrophil recruitment, and evaluated cardiac structure, function, and injury using cardiac
troponin I (cTnI) as a biomarker. These additional findings are now presented in Supplemental
Figure S7.
Regarding neutrophil influx during coronary ligation, it is important to note that neutrophils retain
the ability to access injured cardiac tissue even in the absence of reperfusion (i.e., during
occlusion). These cells can traverse the vascular endothelium in a luminal-to-abluminal direction
to reach the site of injury and contribute to systemic inflammation. This migratory behavior has
been elegantly demonstrated using 4D imaging by the Nourshargh group (PMID: 21706006)
and in vivo imaging by Paul Kubes (PMID: 28983053).
To confirm neutrophil presence in infarcted tissue in our model, we performed
immunohistochemical staining of ischemic WT hearts at 6 hours post-MI and observed robust
neutrophil infiltration, indicated by the presence of multilobulated nuclei (Figure R6). These
findings support the suitability of the LAD ligation model for studying early neutrophil responses
following myocardial injury.
tissue, it is important to emphasize that neutrophils are not cardiac-resident cells like
macrophages; they are recruited only in response to injury (PMID: 31941367). Therefore, the
number of neutrophils remains consistent whether quantified using only infarcted tissue or the
entire ventricle. Flow cytometry, as the most widely accepted method for neutrophil
quantification in the heart, supports this approach (PMID: 28158426, 26358260, 36034743).
Comment -2. The cited references #32, 44, and 50 are not well poised to back up the
statement that “ischemic damage caused by both permanent ligation and reperfusion injury
attracts neutrophils to the infarct”. None of these studies provides histological data on neutrophil
cell infiltration in the myocardium. Moreover, the 37-year-old study by Chatelain et al (ref 50) was performed using a canine model of both ligation and temporary (3h) occlusion and showed
significantly less radiolabeled neutrophils in the infarct region following full ligation (even in a
species with abundant coronary collaterals). Therefore, the limitation reported by the authors
that more temporal studies focusing on earlier time points than 6hrs are required, is not
convincing. To the contrary, additional studies using an ischemia reperfusion model are
indispensable, as well as a larger number of animals per group to increase the power of the
study (at least 10 animals per group rather than 4-6 as is).
Response-2: We acknowledge that some of our initial experiments were underpowered. To
address this limitation, we repeated several key studies, particularly those with fewer than six
mice per group, to strengthen the statistical rigor of our findings. Please see new figures 5L, 5M,
6K, 6J, S1H, S1I, S5H and S5J. Additionally, we now include new immunohistochemical (IHC)
data demonstrating neutrophil infiltration in both reperfused and non-reperfused models at 6
hours post-ischemia (Figure R6). Interestingly, we observed greater neutrophil accumulation in
the infarcted tissue during ischemic-reperfusion injury (50-minute ligation followed by 6-hour
reperfusion) compared to that of permanently ligated MI model, highlighting differences in the
early inflammatory response between these two injury types (Figure R7 and Figure S7).
Comment -3. The histological data presented in figure 5 are very limited and do not allow
proper evaluation of the extent of fibrotic remodeling of the infarcted LV, especially at 30 days
post ligation. One would expect to see full transmural infarction over a large part of the LV free
wall in WT (as suggested by the echo image Fig 5, panel I and as explicitly highlighted in
reference 44).
Response-3: We would like to clarify that we are referring to the extent of transmural infarction.
As shown in Figure 5J (Masson’s Trichrome), the infarct is extensive, encompassing the entire
ventricular wall downstream of the ligation in WT+ MI mice. This observation is further
corroborated by the echocardiographic data, as recommended by the reviewer.
Comment -4. Also, mortality rates are extremely high with only 1 or 2 mice surviving at the 30
day follow up time point. Such high fatality rates do not instill confidence in the experimental
approach when studying novel strategies to regulate what the authors call “runaway
inflammatory responses”.
Response-4: This is partly due to the larger-than-usual infarct size (>30%) induced during
ligation. While we initially started with more than 10 mice per group, the combined effects of
BMT and MI led to significant mortality rates, ranging from 70% in WT mice to 30% in β2 AR KO
mice. High mortality rates are commonly observed in permanent ligation models, and our
findings are consistent with these expected outcomes.
shedding and cell softening is not novel and the finding that MI is capable of inducing a similar
phenomenon is of interest and points toward potential pharmacological interventions to interfere
with this early demargination. Unfortunately, the methodological limitations and lack of outcome
data using beta2-AR blockers do not allow to address our knowledge gaps.
Response: We agree with the reviewer and do not claim that the mechanisms of DEX/NE-
induced demargination (via CD62L shedding or cell softening) are novel. Our experiments were
primarily aimed at identifying a potential target for regulating initial neutrophil recruitment to
prevent the amplification of granulopoiesis, as we recently reported (PMID: 31941367,
34788059). We used butaxamine, a specific β2 blocker, to investigate its effects on neutrophil
demargination and recruitment in mouse models. Additionally, we included propranolol to
assess the translational relevance of our findings to humans, as propranolol and carvedilol are
commonly used in clinical settings post-MI.
Comment-6. The authors report that bone marrow transfer experiments with myeloid cell-
specific ablation of beta 1 and beta1 and beta2 receptors impact on the trafficking to the
infarcted myocardium at 6hrs post ligation (again no convincing data given the methodological
limitations and absence of neutrophil-specific immunohistochemistry) but fail to impact on
survival (staggering mortality rates – see above #4.) or on functional echo parameters.
Unfortunately, more robust MRI imaging data allowing comprehensive function structure
analysis are not available but have become the contemporary standard.
Response-6: We would have delved deeper into characterizing the histological and functional
data if we had identified greater relevance for these studies. The primary objective of these
experiments was to emphasize that long-term depletion of neutrophils, achieved by deleting β1,
β2, or both, is detrimental to cardiac health. These findings align with those observed in studies
involving long-term neutrophil depletion using antibodies (PMID: 28158426) or blocking
neutrophil-derived proteins, such as S100A8/A9 (PMID: 31292614).
Comment-7. The major translational value from this study is the potential role of short-term
inhibition of beta receptor blockade (combined beta1-2 versus selective beta2) on neutrophil
trafficking and subsequent infarct functional and structural remodeling. As presented in figure 6,
it is unclear to this reviewer exactly how many animals were incorporated in the respective
study groups. Again, survival data in the control group do not instill great confidence in the
model and major state of the art diagnostic criteria to evaluate early ischemic burden are
lacking.
Response-7: We initially started with 10 mice per group, but some groups experienced
substantial mortality, with rates as high as 70% in the vehicle-treated group. It is important to
note that these are non-reperfused models, where a mortality rate of 70% in untreated mice is
considered typical. However, short-term treatment with propranolol significantly improved
survival, increasing it to 90%.
Comment-8. The authors should definitely integrate troponin injury markers in their study to
provide more convincing evidence of cardioprotection and rescue of myocardial viable tissue
despite full ligation of nutrient blood supply. In the absence of these corroborating data and
confirmation in a reperfusion model, the data reported here are too preliminary.
Response: Thank you for this suggestion. In response, we conducted additional studies using
both myocardial infarction (MI) and ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) models to evaluate cardiac
troponin I levels at various time points following myocardial injury. These data provide a
quantitative assessment of myocardial injury and allow us to further examine the impact of
short-term (ST) propranolol treatment on cardiac injury, structure, and function. The results
have now been incorporated into the revised manuscript and are presented in Figure S6.
discussion reiterates many sections already discussed in the results. Overall, it can be easily
reduced by 30-40%.
Response: We have substantially shortened the manuscript, particularly the Discussion section
(highlighted), reducing the word count from 2,066 to 1,400 words.
Reviewer 3
Comment #1: Reviewer 3 arguments that insufficient data have been presented of neutrophil
infiltration in the early phase (6h) post MI. Reviewer 3 wants to see more specific
immunohistological data on this aspect. As requested, the authors show in their
immunohistological assessments, that even in the permanently ligated coronary artery MI model
(LAD), myocardial neutrophil infiltration can be observed, which supports the current hypothesis.
In Figure-R7 the authors show that Ly6G-positive infiltrating cells are visible (B) which, however,
is not reflected in the H&E stainings (nucleoli are not really visible in infiltrating cells). Basically,
this is a critical question of Reviewer 3 which needs to be answered in more details and in depth
and not just to provide three histological sections for this critical aspect. Most of the initial
hypothesis relies on the assumption, that early infiltration of neutrophils occurs post-MI and is of
crucial pathophysiological consequence for function and survival thereafter. Thus, the Reviewer
points to a critical issue, but the Response is positive but not totally convincing. Further, these
important data need to be shown and validated in the text and figures of the main manuscript
(not just comments to the Reviewers).
Response: Thank you for emphasizing the importance of rigorously validating early neutrophil
infiltration after MI and for recommending that these data be incorporated into the main
manuscript. While flow cytometry provides a robust and quantitative assessment of cardiac
neutrophils, we complemented these analyses with histology and IHC in response to the
reviewer’s initial concerns. Our Ly6G immunostaining clearly identifies neutrophils within the
myocardium at 6 hours post-MI; although multilobed nuclei are not easily visualized on H&E
sections—likely due to technical limitations in staining or resolution—this does not contradict the

previously provided confocal images (Reviewer Fig. R6) showing Ly6G neutrophils with distinct
multilobed nuclear morphology, further confirming their early presence in the infarcted
myocardium. We have now included this in the manuscript as Suppleme⁺ntal Figure 1C.
To strengthen this conclusion further, we additionally analyzed an independent, publicly
available bulk RNA-seq dataset profiling healthy mouse myocardium (C57BL6) at 6 h and 24 h
after permanent LAD ligation (PMID: 33972017). At 6 h post-MI, we observed significant up-

early neutrophil mobilization and activation and align closely with our flow cytometric and IHC
findings₂. As expected, these pathways were further amplified at 24 h, consistent with the well-
established progression of neutrophil-driven inflammation following MI. We have now
incorporated these transcriptomic analyses (Supplemental Figures 1A and 1B) and expanded
confocal microscopy data (Supplemental Figure 1C) directly into the revised main manuscript.
Together, these orthogonal approaches—flow cytometry, IHC, confocal microscopy, and RNA-
seq provide strong and convergent evidence that neutrophil-driven inflammatory programs are
initiated within the first few hours of myocardial ischemic injury.

accumulation in the I/R model relative to permanent LAD ligation was based on H&E staining,

appropriate method for comparing neutrophil abundance between groups. As the reviewer
correctly notes, the corresponding Ly6G immunostaining which directly identifies neutrophils
showed no significant differences in neutrophil numbers between MI and I/R hearts.
To avoid further confusion, we have removed this reviewer-only figure from the revised
manuscript. Importantly, our goal was not to highlight differences between MI and I/R models,
but rather to demonstrate that cardiac injury, irrespective of model, results in rapid neutrophil
recruitment to the myocardium. Our updated analyses and revised presentation now reflect this
more accurately.
Comment #3: The Reviewer is right to question the histological assessment of fibrosis of the
infarcted LV- myocardium. It is not clear how the scar formation was assessed and calculated. A
more convincing approach seems to be missing still. Usually, gross pathological assessment
and stainings showing cross sections of the whole LV are more adequate.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s request for clearer information regarding how scar
formation and fibrosis were assessed. To clarify, Masson’s trichrome staining was used to
evaluate scar formation, with infarcted regions identified by collagen-rich blue/whitish tissue and
the corresponding loss of viable myocardium. Scar size was quantified as a percentage of the
whole-heart (WH) area using standardized image-analysis workflows. To assess interstitial
fibrosis, we used Picrosirius Red staining, which provides enhanced sensitivity and specificity
for collagen, particularly when viewed under polarized light. These complementary approaches,
Masson’s trichrome for macroscopic scar architecture and Picrosirius Red for detailed collagen-
based fibrosis were applied to whole heart cross-sections, as now described in detail in the
revised Methods section (Please see supplemental document, page 8) . As recommended by
the reviewer, we have also incorporated whole heart/ LV cross-sectional images into the revised
figures to provide a more comprehensive visualization of scar extent and fibrosis. Please see
figures 5, 6 and supplemental figure 7.
Comment #4: The Reviewers argues the low number of MI mice that survived 30-days after
ligation. This is a critical aspect that is not met by the authors response. Thus, the data shown in
figure 7B is not convincing (due to low numbers of survivors. It is also not clear how much
individual mice could be analyzed by means of echocardiographic assessments.
Response: We presume that the reviewer is referring to the Kaplan–Meier survival data shown
in Figure 6B, as there was no Figure 7 in the submitted manuscript. We agree that long-term
survival is an important consideration when evaluating post-MI remodeling. In our model, 30-day
survival ranged from 30% to 90%, depending on the treatment group. Each experimental cohort
was initiated with 16-20 mice, and therefore even under the most conservative condition of
~70% mortality (seen in both the vehicle and LT propranolol groups), approximately 6 mice per
group remained available for echocardiographic assessment at 30 days. This sample size is
well within the norms of murine MI literature and is generally considered sufficient to provide
statistically and scientifically robust echocardiographic data, particularly in permanent LAD
ligation models, where inter-animal variability is typically lower than in I/R models.
To ensure complete transparency, we now explicitly report the exact n-values at each time point
in the Kaplan–Meier curve in the revised manuscript, making the progression of sample sizes
fully traceable.
Reviewer 4
Comment #1. Vascular demargination. This is a critical aspect for the whole hypothesis of the
manuscript and needs to be substantiated. The authors show that dexamethasone elevates
circulating blood neutrophils of cells with low CD62L surface expression. The argument that
“shedding” of CD62L results in demargination seems logical. It might be of interest to directly

samples.
Response: Shedding of L-selectin (CD62L) from activated neutrophils is a well-established
process in human leukocytes and leads to the appearance of soluble CD62L (sCD62L) in the
circulation. In patients with acute myocardial infarction or myocardial ischemia, dynamic
changes in plasma sCD62L levels have been reported and are thought to reflect leukocyte
activation and recruitment to the injured myocardium (PMID: 1044240). Although sCD62L has
not been systematically examined in murine MI models, we followed the reviewer’s suggestion
and directly measured plasma sCD62L in mice subjected to MI or dexamethasone treatment.
In both settings, sCD62L levels were significantly increased and closely paralleled the
expansion of circulating CD62Llow neutrophils. Notably, both MI and dexamethasone induced a
sustained elevation of sCD62L, with peak levels observed at approximately 6 hours post-
treatment, consistent with prolonged neutrophil activation and demargination (please see figure
2, J-L) . These changes were mirrored by corresponding reductions in neutrophil surface CD62L
expression. Together, these findings extend the established biology of CD62L shedding to acute
MI in mice and provide strong mechanistic support for the concept that β-adrenergic activation
promotes neutrophil demargination via CD62L shedding, in agreement with the reviewer’s
recommendation.
Comment #2. It would be of interest to see the effect of norepinephrine on circulating
neutrophils.
Response: Yes, we performed this analysis. We found that norepinephrine (NE) administration
induces rapid neutrophil demargination, accompanied by reduced surface CD62L expression
and a significant, transient increase in plasma soluble CD62L (sCD62L). The NE-induced rise in
sCD62L occurred earlier than that observed after MI or dexamethasone treatment, peaking at
~3 hours and returning toward baseline by 6 hours, in parallel with recovery of neutrophil
surface CD62L expression (Please see Fig 2, H and K). In contrast, MI, which is associated with
sustained sympathetic activation produced a more prolonged elevation of sCD62L. These
findings further support our conclusion that β-adrenergic signaling drives neutrophil mobilization
via CD62L shedding.
Comment #3. Myocardial infiltration of neutrophils. A better description and validation of
neutrophil infiltration in MI by immunohistochemistry in addition to the flow cytometric data will
strengthen the conclusion. Topographical assessment of myocardial infiltration in respect to
ischemic areas etc.
Response: Please see our response to comment 1, Reviewer 3.
Comment #4. Do the authors have data how neutrophils in the early stage of MI alter tissue
inflammation? Do the authors know whether metalloproteinases and extracellular
rearrangement occurs in areas of neutrophil accumulation? What about S100A8/A9 which was
shown by the group to be of significant importance.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. It is well established that
excessive or prolonged neutrophil accumulation in the myocardium can induce collateral tissue
injury through the release of proteolytic enzymes, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)
and other granule-associated proteases. These enzymes contribute to extracellular matrix
degradation, structural destabilization, and amplification of local inflammation during the early
phase of MI (comprehensively reviewed in PMIDs: 3566486, 35410418, 35276496 and others)
Although the primary focus of our study was not to delineate the downstream injury pathways,
these mechanisms have been extensively characterized in prior work. At the same time,
mounting evidence indicates that complete or sustained neutrophil depletion is detrimental, as
neutrophils also play essential roles in the resolution and repair phases of post-MI healing
(PMID: 28158426). A key example is S100A8/A9, which our group and others have shown to
exhibit dual, time-dependent functions:
 early after MI, S100A8/A9 amplifies inflammation and promotes leukocyte recruitment
(PMIDs: 31941367, 34788059 and 32878477)
 whereas later, it supports resolution and macrophage-mediated reparative processes
(PMID: 32434457, 31262614).
Accordingly, the concept proposed in this manuscript—short-term modulation of neutrophil
activity by targeting β-adrenergic receptor–mediated demargination is mechanistically aligned
with this emerging body of work. Similar to the short-term therapeutic window described for
S100A8/A9 blockade by Marinković et al. (PMID: 32434457, 31262614), our data support the
rationale that transient, rather than sustained, neutrophil-directed interventions may attenuate
early injury while preserving reparative functions.
Comment #5. The proteome data is interesting. However, it is not totally clear as shown in
Figure 3, why the proteome data points specifically to the impact of ß-ARs in this context. The
authors might think about to provide some more specific data on the effect of NE and NE plus
propranolol on proteome profile. Was the effect of NE similar than that observe in MI mice?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In our original submission, we
included a detailed explanation of how the proteomic signatures pointed toward GPCR- and β-
adrenergic–mediated cytoskeletal activation in neutrophils during MI. During revision, some of
this mechanistic context was streamlined for brevity, and we appreciate the opportunity to clarify
the direct link between the proteomic data and β-AR signaling.
As presented in the Figures 3 and Figure S3, we performed parallel proteomic profiling of
neutrophils isolated following acute MI, NE administration, and NE plus propranolol treatment.
These data show that NE alone elicits a proteomic program that strongly parallels the MI-
induced state, including activation of pathways governing cytoskeletal remodeling, actin
polymerization, mechanotransduction, immune cell trafficking, and inflammatory signaling.
Importantly, co-treatment with propranolol (a pan–β-AR antagonist) markedly suppressed the
majority of NE-induced pathway activations, demonstrating that these effects are mediated
predominantly through β-adrenergic receptors. The substantial overlap between the MI-induced
and NE-induced proteomic signatures and, the ability of propranolol to abrogate NE-driven
changes provides direct mechanistic evidence that the proteomic alterations observed after MI
reflect β-AR–dependent signaling. Together, these findings support the conclusion that MI
activates a β-AR–mediated cytoskeletal program in circulating neutrophils, and that NE
administration faithfully recapitulates the major MI-associated proteomic features, while
propranolol effectively blocks them. Please see the underlined text in pages 12 and 13 for
updated version of the text.
Comment #6. Figure 5 shows that bone-marrow transplanted wild type mice with ß2- or ß1/ß2-
deficient bone marrow indicate that blood and myocardial neutrophils are decreased following
MI. No effect on cardiac function or survival was found. However, fibrosis was significantly
enhanced in KO mice compared to wild type. This observation is not easy to understand. What
is the interpretation and explanation of this finding?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful question. Our prior work demonstrated that
the early wave of neutrophils recruited to the infarcted heart serves as an essential trigger for
the amplification of bone-marrow granulopoiesis, which peaks around 24 hours post-MI. At that
time, the upstream mechanism driving this early recruitment had not been defined, but we
hypothesized that limiting this initial influx could help tone down the subsequent expansion of
neutrophils and potentially provide a therapeutic window. However, it is now well-recognized
that prolonged or excessive suppression of neutrophils beyond the early inflammatory window
(>3 days post-MI) can be detrimental, as neutrophils play key roles in inflammation resolution,
collagen remodeling, and coordination of reparative macrophage responses. Sustained
neutrophil deficiency is therefore associated with impaired healing and adverse remodeling,
including increased fibrosis.
In the β2- or β1/β2-deficient bone-marrow chimeras, loss of β-AR signaling reduced early
neutrophil demargination and myocardial recruitment, as expected. However, because these
mice lack β-AR signaling throughout both the inflammatory and reparative phases, they exhibit a
sustained reduction in neutrophil influx into the heart. This prolonged deficit likely disrupts the
normal transition to reparative inflammation, impairs appropriate collagen remodeling, and
ultimately leads to the increased fibrosis observed at later time points. In other words, reducing
neutrophil recruitment for longer than the early inflammatory window does not confer additional
benefit and may in fact be detrimental. These findings support the emerging consensus that
short-term modulation of neutrophil activity can be protective, whereas long-term suppression
interferes with healing and promotes adverse structural remodeling.
Comment #7. Short-term administration of propranolol improves survival, function and reduces
fibrosis formation associated with reduced neutrophil infiltration. In contrast, long-term
administration has virtually no effect. Do the authors have data whether LT-propranolol leads to
only an initial neutrophil demargination?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important question. We performed both short-term
(ST) and long-term (LT) propranolol studies to assess the effects of β1/β2-AR blockade on
neutrophil demargination, myocardial recruitment, and downstream cardiac remodeling. As
shown in Figure 4E, short-term propranolol markedly reduces early neutrophil infiltration into the
heart, which in turn improves survival, cardiac function, and limits fibrosis. In contrast, long-term
propranolol continues to suppress neutrophil recruitment well beyond the early inflammatory
window. While this further reduces total neutrophil numbers, it also diminishes the population of
neutrophils required for transition to reparative inflammation, including coordination with
macrophages during resolution and matrix remodeling. Consequently, LT treatment fails to
confer the benefits observed with short-term inhibition.
With respect to the reviewer’s specific question: demargination is an acute event that occurs
within minutes to hours post-MI, and thus both ST and LT propranolol block the initial
demargination response similarly. What differs is the duration of neutrophil suppression: only
short-term, time-limited blockade preserves the subsequent reparative neutrophil functions
necessary for optimal healing.
Comments on the rebuttal to comments of Reviewer 3.
Comment #1 of Reviewer 3
Reviewer 3 arguments that insufficient data have been presented of neutrophil infiltration in the early
phase (6h) post MI. Reviewer 3 wants to see more specific immunohistological data on this aspect. As
requested the authors show in their immunohistological assessments, that even in the permanently
ligated coronary artery MI model (LAD), myocardial neutrophil infiltration can be observed, which
supports the current hypothesis. In Figure-R7 the authors show that Ly6G-positive infiltrating cells are
visible (B) which, however, is not reflected in the H&E stainings (nucleoli are not really visible in
infiltrating cells). Basically, this is a critical question of Reviewer 3 which needs to be answered in more
details and in depth and not just to provide three histological sections for this critical aspect. Most of
the initial hypothesis relies on the assumption, that early infiltration of neutrophils occurs post-MI and
is of crucial pathophysiological consequence for function and survival thereafter.
Thus, the Reviewer points to a critical issue, but the Response is positive but not totally convincing.
Further, these important data need to be shown and validated in the text and figures of the main
manuscript (not just comments to the Reviewers).
Comment #2 of Reviewer 3
The Reviewer criticizes low numbers of animals per group and wants to see a comparison to I/R
myocardium. The authors responded with new experiments including I/R models and claim that
neutrophil infiltration occurs in both MI and I/R. The authors claim from data shown in Figure-R7,
that neutrophil infiltration is higher in the I/R group compared with MI group. However, this is not
confirmed in Figure-R7, part B (missing statistical significance).
Comment #3 of Reviewer 3
The Reviewer is right to question the histological assessment of fibrosis of the infarcted LV-
myocardium. It is not clear how the scare formation was assessed and calculated. A more convincing
approach seems to be missing still. Usually gross pathological assessment and stainings showing cross
sections of the whole LV are more adequate.
Comment #4 of Reviewer 3
Mortality rates. The Reviewers argues the low number of MI mice that survived 30-days after
ligation. This is a critical aspect that is not met by the authors response. Thus, the data shown in
figure 7B is not convincing (due to low numbers of survivors. It is also not clear how much
individual mice could be analyzed by means of echocardiographical assessments.
Comment #5 of Reviewer 3
Comment is justified by not convincingly responded.
Comment #6 of Reviewer 3
Comments are justified. MRI imaging would be a more timely assessment of LV-function and scare
formation. However, it is understandable that MRI imaging is not routinely available everywhere and
logistically complex, especially in mouse models with high mortality rates.
Comment #7 of Reviewer 3
Comment is justified and not convincingly answered.
Comment #8 of Reviewer 3
Determination of troponin levels have been adequately performed and shown.
Comment #9 of Reviewer 3
As suggested by Reviewer 3 the manuscript has been revised, shortened and the discussion has been

In summary, the comments and criticism of Reviewer 3 are well justified, however, only partially and
