## Methods

Mice and Treatments: Male mice (10-12 weeks old) on a C57BL/6 background were used, including wild-type (WT), β2-adrenergic receptor–deficient (β2AR−/−), and β1/β2-adrenergic receptor double-knockout (DKO) mice. WT mice were obtained from The Jackson Laboratory. β2AR−/− and β1/β2AR−/− mice were provided by Dr. Doug Tilley (Temple University). Mice were housed under specific pathogen–free conditions at The Ohio State University (OSU) and the University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center (OUHSC). All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees (IACUC) at each institution (Ohio State University IACUC, protocol #2019A0056); University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center IACUC, protocol #23-067-SFCHX) and were conducted in accordance with the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Animals were monitored daily by trained personnel for general health, signs of distress, and post-procedural recovery. Humane endpoints were applied in accordance with institutional guidelines. Mice were euthanized using carbon dioxide (CO₂) inhalation followed by cervical dislocation to ensure death, in accordance with institutional guidelines. Mice were maintained on standard chow and randomly assigned to experimental groups. All experiments were performed in male mice.

Drugs and Administration: Drug solutions were prepared under sterile conditions and administered according to IACUC-approved protocols. The following agents were used: propranolol (30 mg/kg, i.p.), butoxamine (12.5 mg/kg, i.p.), metoprolol (12.5 mg/kg, i.p.), α-methyl-DL-tyrosine (AMPT; 40 mg/kg, s.c.), dexamethasone (5 mg/kg, i.v.), granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF; 100 mg/kg, i.p.), norepinephrine (2 mg/kg, i.p.), mifepristone (30 mg/kg, s.c.), and 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU; 16 mg/kg, i.p.). Key reagents and resources are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Method Details
Mouse Model of Myocardial Infarction: Myocardial infarction (MI) was induced by permanent ligation of the left anterior descending artery. Twenty-four to 48 hours before surgery, the fur on ventral surface in and around left chest area was cleared off using depilatory cream. Briefly, the mice were anesthetized with 2% isoflurane anaesthesia using a continuous isoflurane delivery system and with an endotracheal tube respiration was controlled with use of a rodent ventilator. A small longitudinal incision (≤5 mm) was made in the center of the throat to locate the trachea for intubation. After confirming the intubation, 4-0 vicryl sutures were used to close the skin in the throat. The line between left pectoralis and major muscles was identified and then an oblique incision (~7mm) was made to expose the heart and left coronary artery. An 8-0 suture (silk or nylon) was placed around the coronary artery and ligated to create the ischemia. Animals were monitored for the depth of anaesthesia at least every 10 to 15 minutes throughout the surgery. After controlling the exhaust pressure to restore the lungs to normal, 5-0 vicryl sutures were used to close the muscle layer while 4-0 vicryl sutures were then to close the skin on the chest. The animals were gradually weaned off the ventilator during recovery from anaesthesia and monitored further to confirm that they have resumed spontaneous respiration in a normal rhythm without assistance during the postoperative period. The sham group underwent the same surgical procedure, except that the ligature was passed under the LAD but not tied. Immediately after surgery, all mice were injected with a long-acting analgesic, buprenorphine. No-MI mice did not undergo either LAD or sham surgery.

Mouse Model of Myocardial Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury (IRI): Myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury was induced in adult male C57BL/6J mice (10–12 weeks old) as previously described, with minor modifications. Briefly, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane (1–2% in oxygen) and placed on a heating pad to maintain body temperature. A left thoracotomy was performed to expose the heart, and a 7-0 silk suture was placed around the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery approximately 1–2 mm below the tip of the left atrium. To induce ischemia, the suture was tightened and secured with a small piece of PE-10 tubing to occlude the LAD for 50 minutes. Ischemia was confirmed by pallor of the left ventricle and ECG changes. After 50 minutes, the ligature was released to allow reperfusion, verified by return of myocardial color. Mice were monitored during the reperfusion period and euthanized at indicated time points for tissue and plasma collection. The sham group underwent the same surgical procedure, except that the ligature was passed under the LAD but not tied. Immediately after surgery, all mice were injected with a long-acting analgesic, buprenorphine. No-MI mice did not undergo either ligation or sham surgery.

Transthoracic Echocardiography: Echocardiography was performed using the Vevo 3100 high-resolution ultrasound imaging system with a MX400 transducer (Visual Sonics Inc., Toronto CA). Mice were sedated with 2% isoflurane and placed on temperature-maintained platform in a supine position. Hair was removed from the chest using depilatory cream, warmed ultrasound transmission gel placed on the chest and left parasternal long axis view and basal short axis views acquired. Ejection fraction, stroke volume and cardiac output were evaluated on the left parasternal long axis view while fractional shortening was calculated from the short axis view using the Vevo 3100 software. Core body temperature was maintained at 37°C using a heated platform and infrared heat lamp throughout the procedure. Mice with heart rates below 400 bpm (beats per minute) were excluded from the analysis.

Bone Marrow Transplants (BMT): WT mice were lethally irradiated (with 13 Gy from a Cesium gamma source in 2 doses separated by 4 hours) and transplanted with BM (5x106 cells) from donor mice. Chimerism was confirmed using either flow cytometry or qRT-PCR analysis of respective proteins/ genes (mRNA) in peripheral blood cells at ~6 weeks after transplantation. Once the chimerism was confirmed, MI was induced as described above.

White Blood Cell (WBC) Counts: Total WBC in freshly collected mouse blood was measured using hematology analyzer (Element HT-5, Heska, Inc.,) or a K2 Fluorescent Viability Cell Counter (Nexcelom Biosciences, MA).

Flow Cytometry Analysis.
Blood and Bone Marrow Leukocytes: Briefly, fresh blood from mice was collected via tail bleeding directly into microcentrifuge tubes containing EDTA (5 mM) using heparin coated capillary tubes and immediately placed on ice. A small amount of blood was set aside for separation of plasma and for analysis of complete blood cell count (CBC) while the remaining blood was transferred to 15 ml centrifuge tubes and red blood cells were lysed using BD Pharm Lyse (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA), washed, rinsed and resuspended in PBS or FACS buffer (Hanks balanced salt solution, HBSS + 0.1% BSA w/v, 5mM EDTA) for staining.

For isolation of BM, femurs and tibias from each mouse were isolated, cleaned and their ends were cut open with a sharp scissor to expose lumen. Bone marrow was flushed with ice cold PBS using a 23-gauge, 10 ml syringe directly through a 40 mM nylon mesh strainer on a 50 ml centrifuge tube. The BM samples were next spun at 300g for 10 min at 4ºC. Following aspiration of supernatant, red blood cells were lysed using RBC lysis buffer, washed twice with PBS, and immediately stained with a fixable Live/Dead marker (1 ml per million cells in 1 ml for 30 minutes, Molecular Probes, Eugene OR). The cells were then washed and resuspended in 100 ml of FACS buffer containing a cocktail of antibodies directed against different types of leukocytes. In experiments that required intracellular staining, the surface labelled cells were fixed and permeabilized with fix/ perm buffer (30 minutes) and then stained with intracellular antibodies (e.g., S100A9, IL1b) in perm/ wash buffer. The stained cells were analyzed on a LSRII flow cytometer using FACS DiVa software or Cytek Northern Lights flow cytometer (Cytek). Once the debris, doublets (by FSC-H vs. FSC-A) and dead cells, leukocytes were identified as described previously12,13. Representative flow cytometry gating strategies used for the identification of leukocyte populations in blood and BM are shown in Supplementary Figure S9.

Heart Leukocytes: For flow cytometric analysis of leukocytes in the heart, a single cell suspension was first prepared. Briefly, hearts were perfused with ice cold PBS to remove blood cells, harvested, cleared of adhering tissues and atria, minced into 2-3 large pieces, transferred to GentleMACS C tubes (Miltenyi Biotec) containing either collagenase type II (1mg/ml) alone or a cocktail of collagenase I (450U/ml), collagenase XI (125U/ml), hyaluronidase type I-s (60U/ml) and DNase (60U/ml) and processed into a fine suspension using a tissue dissociator (GentleMACS Octo Dissociator, Miltenyi Biotec). Digestion was enabled by alternating between dissociation and incubation in a thermomixer (37ºC, 15 minutes each time) with gentle agitation. The single cell suspension was then filtered through a 100 μm strainer into a 50 ml tube, rinsed with FACS buffer, centrifuged at 300g for 10 min at 4ºC. The resultant pellet was washed, resuspended in 1 ml FACS buffer to determine cell count (K2 Cell Counter, Nexcelom Biosciences) followed by staining for Live/Dead marker, surface and intracellular proteins as described above. Data were acquired on Cytek Northern lights or LSR Fortessa flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, San Jose CA) using FACS Diva software, and analysis was performed with FlowJo software (Ashland, OR). Once the doublets (by FSC-H vs. FSC-A) and dead cells (Live vs. Dead) were excluded, neutrophils were identified as CD45+, Ly6Ghi cells and monocytes as CD45+, Ly6G-, F4/80-, CD11b+, CD115+ and further classified as Ly6-Chi and Ly6-Clo cells. Representative flow cytometry gating strategies used for the identification of leukocyte populations in the heart and spleen are shown in Supplementary Figure S10.

Hematopoietic Stem Cells in the BM: Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells from the BM were prepared as described above. After cell count and staining for Live/Dead markers, the cells were resuspended in a cocktail of antibodies first against lineage-committed cells (B220, CD19, CD11b, CD3e, TER-119, CD2, CD8, CD4, Ly6-C/G) followed by markers of stem cells, proliferation (e.g., Ki67) and EdU. Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells were first identified as Lin-, Sca1+ and ckit+ (LSK) while the hematopoietic progenitor subsets were separated by using antibodies to CD16/CD32 (FcgRII/III) and CD34. Common Myeloid Progenitors (CMP) were identified as Lin-, Sca1-, ckit+, CD34int, FcgRII/IIIint, Granulocyte Macrophage Progenitors (GMP) as Lin-, Sca1-, ckit+, CD34int, FcgRII/IIIhi. Common lymphoid progenitors (CLP) were identified as Lin-, Sca1lo, ckitlo and IL7R+ cells. Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) were identified as Lin-, Sca1+, ckit+, CD48- and CD150+. Cellular proliferation in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells was assessed by measuring the incorporation of EdU and /or Ki67 according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Click-iT™ Plus EdU, Molecular Probes, Eugene OR). Flow cytometry was performed using an LSR Fortessa or Cytek Northern Lights (Cytek) using FACS DiVa or SpectroFlo software. All flow cytometry data were analyzed using FlowJo software. Representative flow cytometry gating strategies used for the identification of HSCs and HSPCs in the BM are shown in Supplementary Figure S11.

Confocal Microscopy: Neutrophils from whole blood were sorted using Neutrophil Isolation kit (130-097-658 Miltenyi Biotec), neutrophils were then permeabilized with BD Cytoperm/Cytofix (BD554722), Fc receptors blocked with Fc Block (TruStain FcX PLUS anti-mouse CD16/CD32, 156603, Biolegend) and stained with Phalloidin, Fluorescein isothiocyanate labelled (P5282, Millipore Sigma) for 60mn and mounted using ProLong Gold antifade reagent with DAPI (P36935, Invitrogen). Neutrophil purification efficiency was assessed by flow cytometry (CD45, CD11b, Ly6G). Confocal images were obtained using Olympus FV3000 Multi confocal.

Histology of Heart Sections: The hearts were harvested in diastole with saturated KCl and CdCl (100 mM) injected through the apex into the left ventricular (LV) cavity. The LV apex was then cannulated, and the heart perfused with PBS, followed by 10% buffered formalin at 75 mmHg, with the severed inferior vena cava serving as the outlet. The hearts were then cut into 2-mm cross-sectional slices and processed for paraffin embedding. The slices were cut into 4 μM sections for histologic examination and picrosirius staining. Images were acquired digitally, and the areas measured using NIH Image J software.

Assessment of scar size and fibrosis
Quantification of Infarct Size: Scar size was evaluated using Masson’s trichrome staining. Deparaffinized and rehydrated sections were incubated in Bouin’s solution, followed by sequential staining with Weigert’s iron hematoxylin (nuclei), Biebrich scarlet–acid fuchsin (cytoplasm and muscle), and aniline blue (collagen). Infarcted myocardium was identified by collagen-rich blue/whitish staining with loss of red-stained viable myocardium. Whole-section images were acquired at low magnification. Infarct area was quantified using ImageJ (NIH) by an investigator blinded to genotype and treatment. The entire myocardial cross-section was manually outlined to obtain the whole-heart (WH) area, and the infarct region was traced based on the presence of collagen-rich tissue. Infarct size was calculated using the equation, Infarct Size (%) = (Infarct area/ Whole heart area) X 100.

Fibrosis Assessment: Interstitial and replacement fibrosis were assessed using Picrosirius Red staining. Rehydrated paraffin sections were stained with 0.1% Sirius Red in saturated picric acid and rinsed in acidified water. Sections were imaged under both brightfield and polarized light, the latter allowing visualization of birefringent collagen fibers. Fibrosis was quantified using ImageJ by applying color thresholding to identify Sirius Red–positive collagen. Fibrotic area was expressed as the percentage of total tissue area. At least 2–3 sections per heart and multiple fields per region were analyzed, with all quantification performed blinded to experimental group.

Proteomics
Cell Lysis: Cell pellets were washed with PBS three times before resuspend in 100 µL of 5% SDS buffer in 50 mM TEAB (Triethylammonium bicarbonate) solution. Samples then were vortexed briefly before proceeding to sonication by using the Bioruptor® Pico (Diagenode, Denville, NJ) following manufacturer’s suggested protocol. Briefly, sonication temperature was set at 4C; sonication cycle was set at 30 sec on and 30 sec off. A total of 10 cycles were done for the cell pellets. (Sometimes, DNAs are not sheared well in SDS buffer so a probe homogenizer can be used to shear DNAs in that case). After sonication, samples were centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 15 min at 4°C to remove any remaining insoluble material. Concentration of the proteins were measured using Qubit fluorometer (ThermoFisher Scientific).

Protein Digestion via Strap: 50 µg of the samples were taken for trypsin digestion. 5 µL of 50 mM ABC containing 5 µg/µL DTT was added, and the sample was incubated at 650C for 15 min followed by addition of 5 µL of 50 mM ABC containing 15 µg/µL iodoacetamide (incubated at RT for 15 min in the dark). Samples were then acidified by adding 12% phosphoric acid (1:10 v/v acid to sample). For every 25 µL of samples, 165 µL of TEAB (Triethylammonium bicarbonate, 1M)/MeOH (10:90 v/v) was added and then loaded to S-trap for further washes. Samples were centrifuged at 4000g for 3 min (4C) to remove supernatant. 150 µL of TEAB (Triethylamonium bicarbonate, 1M)/MeOH (10:90 v/v) was added to the trap as wash solution and the trap was washed 3-6 times depends on the initial loading volume. After the final wash, sequencing grade trypsin dissolved in 50 mM TEAB was added and digested O/N at 370C. The following day, peptides were eluted from the trap by adding 40 µL of 50mM TEAB, 0.1% FA and 0.1% FA in Acetonitrile (50:50), sequentially. The sample was pooled together and dried in a vacufuge and resuspended in 20 µL of 50 mM acetic acid. Peptide concentration was determined by nanodrop (A280 nM).

Orbitrap Fusion: Capillary-liquid chromatography-nanospray tandem mass spectrometry (Capillary-LC/MS/MS) of protein identification was performed on a Thermo-Scientific orbitrap Fusion mass spectrometer equipped with an EASY-Spray™ Sources operated in positive ion mode. Samples (6.4µL) were separated on a easy spray nano column (PepmapTM RSLC, C18 3µ 100A, 75µm X150mm Thermo Scientific) using a 2D RSLC HPLC system from Thermo Scientific. Each sample was injected into the µ-Precolumn Cartridge (Thermo Scientific) and desalted with 0.1% Formic Acid in water for 5 minutes. The injector port was then switched to inject, and the peptides were eluted off the trap onto the column. Mobile phase A was 0.1% Formic Acid in water and acetonitrile (with 0.1% formic acid) was used as mobile phase B. Flow rate was set at 300 nL/min. Mobile phase B was increased from 2% to 20% in 105 min and then increased from 20-32% in 10 min and again from 32-95% in 1 min and then kept at 95% for another 4 min before being brought back quickly to 2% in 1 min. The column was equilibrated at 2% of mobile phase B (or 98% A) for 15 min before the next sample injection.

MS/MS data was acquired with a spray voltage of 1.95 KV and a capillary temperature of 305 °C is used. The scan sequence of the mass spectrometer was based on the preview mode data dependent TopSpeed™ method: the analysis was programmed for a full scan recorded between m/z 375-1500 and a MS/MS scan to generate product ion spectra to determine amino acid sequence in consecutive scans starting from the most abundant peaks in the spectrum in the next 3 seconds. To achieve high mass accuracy MS determination, the full scan was performed at FT mode, and the resolution was set at 120,000 with internal mass calibration. Three compensation voltage (cv=-50, -65 and -80v) were used for samples acquisition. The AGC Target ion number for FT full scan was set at 4 x 105 ions, maximum ion injection time was set at 50 ms and micro scan number was set at 1. MSn was performed using HCD in ion trap mode to ensure the highest signal intensity of MSn spectra. The HCD collision energy was set at 32%. The AGC Target ion number for ion trap MSn scan was set at 3.0E4 ions, maximum ion injection time was set at 35 ms and micro scan number was set at 1. Dynamic exclusion is enabled with a repeat count of 1 within 60s and a low mass width and high mass width of 10ppm.

The raw files were searched using Mascot Daemon by Matrix Science version 2.5.1 (Matrix Science, Boston, MA) via ProteomeDiscoverer (Thermo) against the database provided by the user. The mass accuracy of the precursor ion was set to 10 ppm, accidental pick of 113C peaks was also included into the search. The fragment mass tolerance was set to 0.5 Da. Carbamidomethylation (Cys) is used as a fixed modification and considered variable modifications were oxidation (Met) and deamidation (N and Q). Four missed cleavages for the enzyme were permitted. A decoy database was also searched to determine the false discovery rate (FDR) and peptides were filtered according at 1% FDR. Proteins identified with at least two unique peptides were considered as reliable identification. Any modified peptides are manually checked for validation.

Quantitation: Label free quantitation was performed using the spectral count approach, in which the relative protein quantitation is measured by comparing the number of MS/MS spectra identified from the same protein in each of the multiple LC/MSMS datasets. Scaffold (Proteome Software, Portland, OR) was used for data analysis. Student-t test was performed by scaffold to evaluate if the folder change for certain proteins is significant (p<0.05).

Protein inference and bioinformatic analysis: The resulted MS raw data were processed by Proteome Discoverer V2.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), using the UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot Mus musculus reference protein database for protein identification. Search parameters included: enzyme: trypsin; maximum miss cleavages: 2; fixed modification: cysteine carbamidomethylation; variable modifications: oxidation of methionine and deamidation of asparagine and glutamine. The criteria for protein identification also contained the detection of at least 2 unique peptide per protein and the protein false discovery rate (FDR) target to be below 0.05. Label-free relative protein quantitation on the precursor level was performed using the same software platform, which aligns chromatograms, extracts ion peaks and integrates them to compare peptide/protein spectral abundance along the different datasets. We enabled 90% of replicate features and the ANOVA hypothesis test to determine the statistical significance associated with the protein ratio calculation. Normalization was done using the total peptide amount on controls average.

The differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) were identified with an abundance ratio ≥ 1 and an adjusted P-value ≤ 0.05, based on the Benjamini-Hochberg algorithm, was set as the cut-off criterion.

Measurement of Cardiac Troponin I (cTnI) Levels
Plasma samples were collected from mice at designated time points following myocardial infarction (MI) or IR, with or without propranolol treatment. Cardiac troponin I levels were quantified using the Mouse Cardiac Troponin I (TNNI3) ELISA Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# EEL112), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Concentrations were determined using a standard curve generated from known calibrators provided with the kit.

Measurement of soluble CD62L Levels
The levels of soluble L-selectin (sCD62L) were measured in the plasma of the indicated groups at various time points using a commercially available ELISA kit (The RayBio Mouse L-Selectin, Cat# ELM-L-Selectin). Plasma samples were diluted 200-fold before incubation. The plasma levels of the unknown samples were determined based on the standard curve generated using known mouse L-selectin protein standards.

Western Blot Analysis in heart tissue
Mouse left ventricular area was dissected and used for the protein extraction using RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with complete protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail. The lysate was mixed with NuPAGE lds sample buffer and heat denatured at 75Soc for 10-15 min. The proteins were separated using 10 or 12% NuPAGE Bis-Tris gels and transferred onto a PVDF membrane. Further, the membrane was blocked with 3% BSA for 30-60 min at room temperature. The membrane was probed for the indicated targets ( -SMA (ThermoFisher, #14-9760-82, 1:1000), p-ERK (CST, #4370S, 1:1000), T-ERK (CSIT, #4695S, 1:1000 and GAPDH (CST, #5174S, 1:1000) and developed using SuperSignal™ West Femto Maximum Sensitivity Substrate and captured/visualized using LI-COR odyssey XF system.

Gene expression analysis
Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) experiments in LV of hearts were performed using TaqMan assays for target genes (Col1a1 assay ID: Mm00801666_g1; Col3a1 assay ID: Mm00802296_g1; FN1 assay ID: Mm01256744_m1) using TaqMan Fast Advanced Master Mix (ThermoFisher). Changes in the expression levels of target genes were determined using Comparative CT (ΔΔCT) analysis, with 18S (ThermoFisher #4319413E) acting as an endogenous control.

Statistical Analysis: Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Comparisons between two groups were performed using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test for normally distributed data or a Mann–Whitney test for non-normally distributed data. Comparisons among three or more groups were analyzed using one- or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Holm–Šidák or Tukey’s multiple comparisons tests, as appropriate. Non-parametric multi-group comparisons were performed using the Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test. Survival analyses were conducted using the log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test. Longitudinal data (e.g., echocardiography measurements) were analyzed using two-way ANOVA with a mixed-effects model to account for missing values due to post-MI mortality, followed by Bonferroni’s multiple comparisons test. All statistical tests were two-sided unless otherwise specified. A two-sided P value ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (version 8). Extended methodological details are provided in the Supplementary Information.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript by Dahdah et al. presents a comprehensive study on the early recruitment of neutrophils to the ischemic heart following myocardial infarction (MI), focusing on the role of vascular demargination rather than granulopoiesis in the bone marrow (BM) or spleen. Neutrophil demargination is a process by which neutrophils are mobilized from the vascular wall into the bloodstream. The authors employ a variety of advanced methodologies, including sophisticated in vivo experiments, flow cytometry, confocal microscopy, and proteomics to elucidate the signalling pathways that regulate neutrophil demargination and subsequent recruitment to the infarct. Specifically, they explored the role of β-adrenergic receptor (β-AR) signalling in mediating this process.

The research is novel, and the findings are of significant interest, as they provide insights into the temporal dynamics of neutrophil recruitment and highlight the potential of targeted pharmacological intervention in early MI management.
However, I would recommend a revision to further strengthen the mechanistic understanding of neutrophil demargination and the potential for therapeutic intervention.

The use of dexamethasone (DEX) and norepinephrine (NE) as demarginating agents in mice needs careful consideration. While these agents can induce demargination, they may also have additional systemic effects, including influencing the behavior of other immune cells, eg:
Macrophages: Dexamethasone can inhibit the activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production of macrophages, promoting a more anti-inflammatory phenotype.
T cells: Dexamethasone can suppress T cell proliferation and cytokine production, leading to reduced inflammation.
Dendritic cells: Dexamethasone can impair dendritic cell maturation and antigen presentation, thereby reducing T cell activation.
Furthermore, TBI has a big impact on the other immune cell populations and it can not be ruled out, that the observed effects are due to altered interactions between neutrophils and macrophages, DCs and T cells.
Therefore, when using TBI , BM chimeric approaches and dexamethasone as a tool to study neutrophil demargination, it is crucial to consider its potential effects on other immune cell populations.
To isolate the specific effects on neutrophils, comparing the effects of dexamethasone on neutrophil demargination in TBI wild-type mice to those after ablation of specific immune cell types (using e.g., macrophage-depleted mice or CD11c-cell depleted mice) could help to elucidate the direct and indirect effects of dexamethasone.
To control for these effects, it is also recommended to measure systemic inflammatory markers (e.g., cytokines) after DEX and NE administration.
Please also consider to discuss whether the observed demargination is a localized response (specific to ischemic tissue) or part of a systemic phenomenon. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms underlying neutrophil demargination in MI, it would be beneficial to explore the interplay between β-AR signalling and other relevant pathways, such as those mediated by chemokines and adhesion molecules. Additionally, considering the long-term consequences of excessive neutrophil recruitment, such as impaired tissue repair and adverse cardiac remodelling, would provide valuable insights into the clinical implications of the authors findings.
To directly measure β2-AR activation in neutrophils, phospho-specific antibodies (to measure phosphorylated proteins downstream of the receptor, e.g., p-ERK1/2, p-Akt, p-p38 MAPK) should be employed in isolated neutrophils stimulated with a β2-adrenergic agonist like isoproterenol or inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and CXCL8) to mimic the inflammatory response. This could provide further evidence for the role of β2-ARs in mediating neutrophil demargination.
To complement the proteomics analysis of demarginated neutrophils post- MI or NE administration, which revealed the activation of processes involved in cellular movement and cytoskeletal reorganization, visualizing changes in cellular morphology and cytoskeletal reorganization would provide additional insights. Immunofluorescence microscopy should be used to show changes in cell shape, formation of pseudopodia, and cytoskeletal dynamics in response to β-AR activation.

Minor:
Figure 5 j,k and Figure 6 h,i: Please check your scale bars! From my point of view, magnifications are not the same, so the scale bars cannot be the same size!

### Reviewer 2

In this paper the authors propose that neutrophil demargination induced by NE via beta-2 adrenergic receptors, rather than neutrophil production and mobilization from the BM or spleen, is responsible for the first wave of neutrophil infiltration in the heart after myocardial infarction in mice. Figure 1 examines kinetics of granulopoiesis and granulocyte dynamics in various compartments i.e. BM blood spleen heart, showing that peak heart infiltration occurs before peak granulopoiesis suggesting non-BM/spleen source of neutrophils for early recruitment. Figure 2 uses a model of total body irradiation to disrupt granulopoiesis, and treat mice with demargination inducing agents (DEX, NE), providing data supporting the notion that demarginating neutrophils are recruited to the heart early after MI. In Figure 3 the authors performed proteomics analysis of blood neutrophil 6 hours after MI or NE and NE+propranolol treatment. Figure 4/5: the authors use various treatments to prevent NE synthesis of block different beta adrenergic receptors (Fig 4) or use mice with myeloid specific deficiency in beta2 or beta1+beta2 AR (Fig 5), proposing a role of beta2-AR in neutrophil demargination and recruitment to the heart after MI. Figure 6 shows that short term, but not long term, propranolol treatment improves cardiac repair after permanent MI in mice.

The paper is clearly written, the proposed conclusions are an important and a new contribution to the field. There are however several technical and conceptual issues, including insufficiently powered experiments and unexpected results in the LAD permanent ligation model. I would furthermore suggest toning down the conclusions as most evidence is indirect, and discuss the weaknesses and limitation of the different experimental approaches in more details.

-One weakness of the paper is that it is technically not possible to clearly distinguish neutrophil origin and most of the provided evidence is indirect. Thus, most of the conclusion are overstated e.g. line 155 “Since we found no role for either BM or spleen”. While experiments such as those presented in Figure 1 are informative, they only provide indirect evidence as the different compartments observed are not merely ‘communicating vases’, and the number of neutrophils at a given time point in the BM represents a complex balance between production, retention, mobilization and reverse-migration. The EdU experiments show neutrophils originating from HSPCs that have proliferated during the labeling period, but mature neutrophils originating from BM or spleen reservoirs and mobilized early after MI cannot be distinguished from demarginating neutrophils. However, the cumulative amount of evidence provided by the authors indeed suggests that demargination is a substantial source of early neutrophil recruitment to the heart.
-Figure 1A-B: please show pre-gating strategy. There is possibly an error in percentages showed as they are exactly the same between heart and blood
-The authors conclude that neutrophil numbers are not affected in the BM at 6 hours but the data shown in Figure 1E is not very robust, the experiment being insufficiently powered with clear outlier observations.
-Line 182: “wherein the blood neutrophil count is slightly decreased”. According to Figure S1D the neutrophil count might be close to 0 at 18h, but there is actually no measurement performed at this time point
-Neutrophil counts in the bone marrow and spleen should be provided for all interventions.
-Many experiments are quite underpowered with sometimes as few as n=3 for functional readouts in a model known for its quite substantial variability. Interexperiment variability also seems quite high with e.g. a very wide range of reported blood neutrophil counts in the control groups across experiments.
-Figure 6B shows a 90% death rate in the control MI group, this is rather unusual in this model. The effect of short-term propranolol treatment with almost no scar formation after LAD ligation (Figure 6H-K) also does not seem very realistic, this would represent a spectacular cardioprotective effect in this permanent ischemia model. Whether and how blinding and randomization were performed is not indicated in the methods.
-The methods do not mention the use of analgesics prior to or after MI surgery.
-Previous work showing splenic retention of immune cells in mice with myeloid beta2-AR deficiency early (24 hours) after MI suggests that some of the effects observed here might also be caused by splenic or medullar retention of neutrophils.
-Assessment of neutrophil purity after magnetic sorting for proteomics studies is missing
-Full list of differentially abundant proteins to provide as supplementary table, here only unannotated heatmap + pathway analyses are shown. It would be a good addition to provide some cross-validation of proteomics and flow cytometry data e.g. do the authors see downregulation of CD62L in the proteomics data, and can some up/down proteins identified by proteomics be validated by flow?
-Lines 307-308: ‘Administration of NE resulted in the activation of an immune response that was very similar to that induced by MI’ : how was this formally quantified? Overlap of up/down proteins induced by MI or NE?

### Reviewer 3

In this report Dahdah and colleagues set out to investigate the mechanisms whereby neutrophils are supplied to the heart in the early hours after myocardial infarction as part of the complex innate immune response to ischemic injury. Because myocardial infiltration of neutrophils is thought to occur much quicker than granulopoiesis in the bone marrow, the authors hypothesized that the early wave of neutrophils recruited to the heart is exclusively sourced from the vasculature (the marginating pool) and not from increased production in the bone marrow or release from the spleen. Using a combination of flow cytometry, BM ablation of hematopoietic stem cells, confocal microscopy and multiple proteomics analysis, they propose that the MI-evoked neutrophilia is mediated by a demargination process. Finally, using genetic and pharmacological strategies (they report that suppression of norepinephrine synthesis or disruption of β-adrenergic signaling reduced both neutrophil demargination and recruitment to the heart, while only short-term inhibition of β-ARsignaling improved cardiac remodeling and function in mice subjected to permanent LAD ligation.

General comments
Overall, the central research question in this study evolves on the innate immune response after ischemic myocardial damage and the specific role of one of the early responders in this process, the neutrophils. The inflammatory response after MI is required for the induction of cardiac repair processes to which many cell types contribute and has received ample attention over the past 2 decades in both preclinical and a myriad of clinical studies. Disappointingly, all interventional studies targeting the immune response in the acute setting of MI have failed highlighting the need for a better mechanistic understanding of key molecular and cellular pathways driving either myocardial damage or repair. The authors state that deciphering the signaling pathways that stimulate the demargination of neutrophils and their recruitment to the ischemic heart may provide a viable approach to regulate neutrophil trafficking to the heart post-MI and conclude that their “findings support a pharmacological strategy to contain the initial onslaught of neutrophils on the ischemic heart using β2-AR blockers to regulate the otherwise runaway inflammatory response”.

While in general the topic addresses a timely problem and while the demargination hypothesis of neutrophil trafficking post MI is supported by experimental data, the study suffers from many methodological limitations and flaws. At face value the additional knowledge brought to the field by the data as presented is at best incremental as the proper experimental design to identify the role of beta2-AR blockers in the response to acute myocardial infarction and their impact on neutrophil trafficking to the heart remains elusive.

Specific comments.
1. A major limitation of the study is the use of the permanent ligation of the LAD to induce myocardial infarction in mice, a species devoid of collateral coronary circulation (which in contrast is abundantly present in the canine model). Full LAD ligation will prevent influx of inflammatory cells (neutrophils and monocytes) in the infarcted area in the first few hours after ligation, despite the statements to the contrary by the authors. They do not provide any histological data at 6h post MI that would corroborate the presumed influx of neutrophils in the infarct territory. The FACS data, listed in figure 1 to underpin their claim, do not provide the required scientific evidence to substantiate this critical statement, as the data are derived from whole LV homogenates. The authors need to provide histological sections prepared at 6h post MI and stain for the presence of infiltrating neutrophils. They should next (semi)quantitate the degree of trafficking in their subsequent studies with different pharmacological and genetic interventions.
2. The cited references #32, 44, and 50 are not well poised to back up the statement that “ischemic damage caused by both permanent ligation and reperfusion injury attracts neutrophils to the infarct”. None of these studies provides histological data on neutrophil cell infiltration in the myocardium. Moreover, the 37-year-old study by Chatelain et al (ref 50) was performed using a canine model of both ligation and temporary (3h) occlusion and showed significantly less radiolabeled neutrophils in the infarct region following full ligation (even in a species with abundant coronary collaterals). Therefore, the limitation reported by the authors that more temporal studies focusing on earlier time points than 6hrs are required, is not convincing. To the contrary, additional studies using an ischemia reperfusion model are indispensable, as well as a larger number of animals per group to increase the power of the study (at least 10 animals per group rather than 4-6 as is).
3. The histological data presented in figure 5 are very limited and do not allow proper evaluation of the extent of fibrotic remodeling of the infarcted LV, especially at 30 days post ligation. One would expect to see full transmural infarction over a large part of the LV free wall in WT (as suggested by the echo image Fig 5, panel I and as explicitly highlighted in reference 44).
4. Also, mortality rates are extremely high with only 1 or 2 mice surviving at the 30 day follow up time point. Such high fatality rates do not instill confidence in the experimental approach when studying novel strategies to regulate what the authors call “runaway inflammatory responses”.
5. The finding that DEX and NE contribute to neutrophil demargination via CD62L shedding and cell softening is not novel and the finding that MI is capable of inducing a similar phenomenon is of interest and points toward potential pharmacological interventions to interfere with this early demargination. Unfortunately, the methodological limitations and lack of outcome data using beta2-AR blockers do not allow to address our knowledge gaps.
6. The authors report that bone marrow transfer experiments with myeloid cell-specific ablation of beta 1 and beta1 and beta2 receptors impact on the trafficking to the infarcted myocardium at 6hrs post ligation (again no convincing data given the methodological limitations and absence of neutrophil-specific immunohistochemistry) but fail to impact on survival (staggering mortality rates – see above #4.) or on functional echo parameters. Unfortunately, more robust MRI imaging data allowing comprehensive function structure analysis are not available but have become the contemporary standard.
7. The major translational value from this study is the potential role of short term inhibition of beta receptor blockade (combined beta1-2 versus selective beta2) on neutrophil trafficking and subsequent infarct functional and structural remodeling. As presented in figure 6, it is unclear to this reviewer exactly how many animals were incorporated in the respective study groups. Again survival data in the control group do not instill great confidence in the model and major state of the art diagnostic criteria to evaluate early ischemic burden are lacking. The authors should definitely integrate troponin injury markers in their study to provide more convincing evidence of cardioprotection and rescue of myocardial viable tissue despite full ligation of nutrient blood supply. In the absence of these corroborating data and confirmation in a reperfusion model, the data reported here are too preliminary.
8. The manuscript is excessively long and, in many instances, repetitious. The discussion reiterates many sections already discussed in the results. Overall, it can be easily reduced by 30-40%.

may also have additional systemic effects, including influencing the behavior of other immune
cells, e.g.:
Macrophages: Dexamethasone can inhibit the activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine
production of macrophages, promoting a more anti-inflammatory phenotype.
T cells: Dexamethasone can suppress T cell proliferation and cytokine production, leading to
reduced inflammation.
Dendritic cells: Dexamethasone can impair dendritic cell maturation and antigen presentation,
thereby reducing T cell activation.
Furthermore, TBI has a big impact on the other immune cell populations, and it cannot be ruled
out, that the observed effects are due to altered interactions between neutrophils and
macrophages, DCs and T cells. Therefore, when using TBI , BM chimeric approaches and
dexamethasone as a tool to study neutrophil demargination, it is crucial to consider its potential
effects on other immune cell populations.
To isolate the specific effects on neutrophils, comparing the effects of dexamethasone on
neutrophil demargination in TBI wild-type mice to those after ablation of specific immune cell
types (using e.g., macrophage-depleted mice or CD11c-cell depleted mice) could help to
elucidate the direct and indirect effects of dexamethasone.
To control for these effects, it is also recommended to measure systemic inflammatory markers
(e.g., cytokines) after DEX and NE administration.
Response-2: We fully agree with the reviewer that dexamethasone exhibits potent anti-
inflammatory properties and is widely used as an anti-inflammatory agent in various clinical
settings. However, it is important to emphasize that these effects generally manifest after
prolonged corticosteroid treatment. In our studies, dexamethasone was used solely as a
neutrophil demarginating agent in conjunction with NE as an experimental tool. Our data is
consistent with data from a recent study in humans that showed successful application of both
DEX and NE as demarginating agents (PMID: 26858400) to elucidate the mechanisms of
neutrophil demargination.
point that interactions between neutrophils and macrophages, DCs, and T cells cannot be ruled
out. However, TBI is primarily used in our models to deplete stem cells to completely halt
granulopoiesis. Despite the absence of routine granulopoiesis, both MI induction and DEX
administration were still able to increase circulating neutrophil numbers, suggesting that
marginated (matured cells that were not killed by TBI) neutrophils serve as the primary source
of neutrophils in the heart immediately after MI. While it remains challenging to determine
whether this increase results from interactions between neutrophils and other immune cells, our
study primarily aimed to identify the sources of neutrophils post-MI. That said, we cannot
completely exclude the involvement of other cytokines in neutrophil demargination during DEX
and NE treatment. As suggested by the reviewer, we conducted a cytokine array to evaluate
systemic inflammatory markers following DEX/ NE treatment. The resulting data are presented
in Table 1. As shown in the Table 1, DEX/NE treatment for 6 hours has no significant impact on
any of the major cytokines tested. We also present serum cytokine data (Table -2) in sham and
MI mice at different time points post-MI to show how MI increase certain inflammatory cytokines
as early as 6 hours but not DEX or NE.
Comment-3. Please also consider discussing whether the observed demargination is a
localized response (specific to ischemic tissue) or part of a systemic phenomenon. To gain a
more comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms underlying neutrophil demargination in
MI, it would be beneficial to explore the interplay between β-AR signaling and other relevant
pathways, such as those mediated by chemokines and adhesion molecules. Additionally,
considering the long-term consequences of excessive neutrophil recruitment, such as impaired
tissue repair and adverse cardiac remodeling, would provide valuable insights into the clinical
implications of the authors findings.
Response-3: This is an important point. As suggested, we have included this in our discussion
under the limitations (Page 20). We believe that neutrophil demargination represents a systemic
response driven by sympathetic nervous system (SNS) activation. However, it is likely triggered
by ischemic damage (i.e., MI) to the heart, as sham surgeries—while likely activating the SNS
to some extent—did not cause a similar neutrophil demargination response.
The interplay between β-AR signaling and those mediated by chemokines and adhesion
molecules is indeed complex, and defining this interplay in detail is beyond the scope of this
study. Indeed, it is well established that chemokines and cytokines activate the endothelium,
promoting the adhesion of leukocytes to the vessel wall. In contrast, β-adrenergic receptor (β-
AR) stimulation on neutrophils promotes their migration away from the endothelium by
suppressing the expression of adhesion molecules. This facilitates neutrophil movement into
both the circulation and the affected tissues. The delicate balance between adhesion and
migration is critical for regulating neutrophil trafficking during inflammatory responses and
ensuring proper immune responses without excessive tissue damage.
Regarding the long-term consequences of neutrophil recruitment, previous studies, including
our own, have shown that excessive neutrophil infiltration into the heart can exacerbate infarct
expansion and impair cardiac remodeling (PMID:31941367). On the other hand, indiscriminate
depletion of neutrophils beyond the inflammatory phase post-MI (after day 3) may negatively
affect wound healing. The findings presented in this manuscript are particularly significant, as
they identify β2 ARs as a promising therapeutic target to modulate excessive neutrophil
recruitment to the heart, particularly in the critical early hours following MI.
Comment-4. To directly measure β2-AR activation in neutrophils, phospho-specific antibodies
(to measure phosphorylated proteins downstream of the receptor, e.g., p-ERK1/2, p-Akt, p-p38
MAPK) should be employed in isolated neutrophils stimulated with a β2-adrenergic agonist like
2
isoproterenol or inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and CXCL8) to
mimic the inflammatory response. This could provide further evidence for the role of β2-ARs in
mediating neutrophil demargination.
Response: This is an important consideration, as neutrophils express a range of cytokine
receptors that could influence their behavior during demargination. To explore this, we
conducted immunoblotting studies using representative ligands: isoproterenol (a β-adrenergic
receptor agonist), TNF-α (a pro-inflammatory cytokine), and CXCL1 (a chemokine that signals
through CXCR1 and CXCR2). Notably, mice do not express CXCL8; instead, they produce
GCP-2/LIX, which also signals via CXCR1/2. Therefore, we used CXCL1 to mimic relevant
chemokine signaling. As shown in Figure-R1, stimulation of bone marrow neutrophils with these
ligands for 6 hours did not induce activation of ERK, AKT, or p38 MAPK pathways. In fact,
phosphorylation of some signaling proteins (e.g., P-AKT) was reduced following treatment with
TNF-α, CXCL1, or isoproterenol. These results suggest that MAPK pathways are unlikely to
mediate neutrophil demargination in response to cytokine or β2-adrenergic receptor activation.
This conclusion is further supported by our proteomics data (Supplemental Figure 2), which
showed no enrichment of MAPK pathway activation despite general GPCR engagement.
Instead, we observed significant changes in proteins involved in actin polymerization and
cytoskeletal remodeling, particularly through calcium-regulated pathways. These included Rac,
Pak, Rho, as well as key regulators of cell polarity and motility such as ROCK, Cofilin (CFN),
Profilin, and LIM kinase (LIMK). Collectively, these findings support a model in which β2-AR-
and cytokine-driven neutrophil demargination is primarily mediated through cytoskeletal and
calcium-dependent signaling rather than MAPK activation.
Comment-5. To complement the proteomics analysis of demarginated neutrophils post- MI or
NE administration, which revealed the activation of processes involved in cellular movement
and cytoskeletal reorganization, visualizing changes in cellular morphology and cytoskeletal
reorganization would provide additional insights. Immunofluorescence microscopy should be
used to show changes in cell shape, formation of pseudopodia, and cytoskeletal dynamics in
response to β-AR activation.
Response-5: Previous studies (PMID: 26858400) have demonstrated that cytoskeletal
reorganization—specifically changes in F-actin intensity and its localization—can reliably
indicate neutrophil motility in response to DEX or NE stimulation. While we acknowledge the
reviewer’s suggestion to include additional markers, we believe that incorporating them would
not significantly change the primary conclusions of our study. Nonetheless, to address this
feedback, we performed additional immunofluorescence staining on mouse blood cells treated
ex vivo with either PBS or NE for 6 hours. As shown in Figure-R2, NE stimulation led to a
pronounced spreading of F-actin and the formation of pseudopodia, consistent with cytoskeletal
remodeling. These findings support the conclusion that β-adrenergic receptor (β-AR) activation
by NE promotes cytoskeletal reorganization, a hallmark of neutrophil motility and migration.
Comment-6: Figure 5 j,k and Figure 6 h,i: Please check your scale bars! From my point of view,
magnifications are not the same, so the scale bars cannot be the same size!
Response: Thank you for bringing this to our attention. We have now corrected the error and
included the appropriate scale bar.
Comment-1: In this paper the authors propose that neutrophil demargination induced by NE via
beta-2 adrenergic receptors, rather than neutrophil production and mobilization from the BM or
spleen, is responsible for the first wave of neutrophil infiltration in the heart after myocardial
infarction in mice. Figure 1 examines kinetics of granulopoiesis and granulocyte dynamics in
various compartments i.e. BM blood spleen heart, showing that peak heart infiltration occurs
before peak granulopoiesis suggesting non-BM/spleen source of neutrophils for early
recruitment. Figure 2 uses a model of total body irradiation to disrupt granulopoiesis, and treat
mice with demargination inducing agents (DEX, NE), providing data supporting the notion that
demarginating neutrophils are recruited to the heart early after MI. In Figure 3 the authors
performed proteomics analysis of blood neutrophil 6 hours after MI or NE and NE+propranolol
treatment. Figure 4/5: the authors use various treatments to prevent NE synthesis of block
different beta adrenergic receptors (Fig 4) or use mice with myeloid specific deficiency in beta2
or beta1+beta2 AR (Fig 5), proposing a role of beta2-AR in neutrophil demargination and
recruitment to the heart after MI. Figure 6 shows that short term, but not long term, propranolol
treatment improves cardiac repair after permanent MI in mice.
The paper is clearly written, the proposed conclusions are an important and a new contribution
to the field. There are however several technical and conceptual issues, including insufficiently
powered experiments and unexpected results in the LAD permanent ligation model. I would
furthermore suggest toning down the conclusions as most evidence is indirect and discuss the
weaknesses and limitation of the different experimental approaches in more details.
Response-1: We appreciate the constructive feedback and thank you for your suggestion. We
have repeated most of the previously underpowered experiments and have included new
figures. Additionally, we have addressed the limitations of the LAD model and have refined our
conclusions accordingly.
Comment-2: One weakness of the paper is that it is technically not possible to clearly
distinguish neutrophil origin and most of the provided evidence is indirect. Thus, most of the
conclusion are overstated e.g. line 155 “Since we found no role for either BM or spleen”. While
experiments such as those presented in Figure 1 are informative, they only provide indirect
evidence as the different compartments observed are not merely ‘communicating vases’, and
the number of neutrophils at a given time point in the BM represents a complex balance
between production, retention, mobilization and reverse-migration. The EdU experiments show
neutrophils originating from HSPCs that have proliferated during the labeling period, but mature
neutrophils originating from BM or spleen reservoirs and mobilized early after MI cannot be
distinguished from demarginating neutrophils. However, the cumulative amount of evidence
provided by the authors indeed suggests that demargination is a substantial source of early
neutrophil recruitment to the heart.
Response-2: We completely agree with the reviewer. Delineating the various mechanisms by
which neutrophils are sourced from different compartments and recruited to the heart post-MI is
indeed challenging. As the reviewer correctly pointed out, the number of neutrophils in
circulation at any given time reflects a delicate balance between their production, mobilization,
retention, and elimination.
Notably, our total body irradiation (TBI) studies provide crucial evidence that mature neutrophils
(protected from radiation) are mobilized from the vasculature during bone marrow ablation. We
appreciate the reviewer’s recognition that our findings support the notion that demargination is a
significant source of early neutrophil recruitment to the heart.
Comment-3: Figure 1A-B: please show pre-gating strategy. There is possibly an error in
percentages showed as they are exactly the same between heart and blood
blood and heart have now been included. Additionally, we have provided the gating strategy for
the data in figures1A and B (Figure. R3).
Comment-4: -The authors conclude that neutrophil numbers are not affected in the BM at 6
hours, but the data shown in Figure 1E is not very robust, the experiment being insufficiently
powered with clear outlier observations.
Response-4: A slight reduction in neutrophil numbers was observed at 6 hours post-myocardial
infarction (MI) compared to the Sham group; however, this difference was not statistically
significant. We repeated the experiment, and similar results were obtained (Figure 1E).
Importantly, inclusion of these additional data points did not alter the overall statistical outcome.
Comment-5: Line 182: “wherein the blood neutrophil count is slightly decreased”. According to
Figure S1D the neutrophil count might be close to 0 at 18h, but there is actually no
measurement performed at this time point
Response: That is correct. Both neutrophil and total WBC counts drastically decrease following
bone marrow ablation. Please note that since we were able to completely deplete neutrophils by
12 hours, we did not measure them again to avoid causing unnecessary stress to the irradiated
animals. Additionally, the 18-hour time point was selected carefully after several preliminary
studies to identify a time when neutrophils are completely depleted without resulting in mortality
in the mice.
Comment-6: Neutrophil counts in the bone marrow and spleen should be provided for all
interventions.
Response-6: Thank you for the suggestion. We do have data on neutrophil counts in both the
bone marrow and spleen for all treatments. These results have now been included in Figure-R4
for completeness.
Comment-7: Many experiments are quite underpowered with sometimes as few as n=3 for
functional readouts in a model known for its quite substantial variability. Interexperiment
variability also seems quite high with e.g. a very wide range of reported blood neutrophil counts
in the control groups across experiments.
Response-7: Yes, some of our initial histological analyses were underpowered due to
unanticipated loss of animals during surgery, which prevented us from reaching the originally
planned group sizes. To address this, we have repeated the experiments and included
additional animals in the previously underpowered groups to strengthen the robustness and
reliability of the results. Please see figures 1, 2, 4, 5L-M, 6J-K and supplementary figures S1H,
S1I, S5I and S5J with new statistical analysis.
Comment-8: Figure 6B shows a 90% death rate in the control MI group, this is rather unusual
in this model. The effect of short-term propranolol treatment with almost no scar formation after
LAD ligation (Figure 6H-K) also does not seem very realistic, this would represent a spectacular
cardioprotective effect in this permanent ischemia model. Whether and how blinding and
randomization were performed is not indicated in the methods.
Response-8: Please note that Figure 6B shows 70% mortality (not 90%) in the control MI
group. This is quite typical, as the untreated mice experience extensive ventricular damage,
such as thinning and rupture. Additionally, our MI surgeries resulted in a large infarct size.
Regarding the short-term propranolol treatment, these data are not entirely surprising, as
neutrophils are the first cells to arrive at the infarct site, and their presence influences the
subsequent inflammatory response. This leads to the secretion of various proteases, which in
turn contribute to cardiac tissue damage. We believe that by preventing excessive neutrophil
5
infiltration, we could reduce the extent of damage to the heart. Please note that these mice were
administered a dose of propranolol 8 hours prior to MI induction as part of a preemptive
strategy. Regarding blinding and randomization, the IHC data were performed by a technician
(Nitin), while surgeries were conducted by Dr. Park, and drugs were injected by Dr. Dahdah.
Although Dr. Dahdah was aware of the group assignments and drugs, the technician was
blinded to the group allocations.
Comment-9: The methods do not mention the use of analgesics prior to or after MI surgery.
Response-9: We apologize for any oversight. We used a long-acting analgesic
(Buprenorphine) for all our MI surgeries, and this information has now been included in the
methods section. Please see supplemental file page 3.
Comment-10: Previous work showing splenic retention of immune cells in mice with myeloid
beta2-AR deficiency early (24 hours) after MI suggests that some of the effects observed here
might also be caused by splenic or medullar retention of neutrophils.
Response-10: While we acknowledge previous studies reporting splenic retention of immune
cells in mice with myeloid β2-AR deficiency early after MI, it is unclear whether this mechanism
is relevant to our model. We quantified neutrophil numbers in both the BM and spleen of β2⁻/⁻
and DKO mice at 6 hours and 30 days post-MI. As shown in Figure R5, there were no
statistically significant differences at either time point. These findings suggest that neutrophil
retention in these reservoirs does not account for the reduced neutrophil numbers observed in
the heart or blood post-MI in β2 BMT mice. This interpretation is further supported by prior data
showing that NE injections do not mobilize neutrophils from the BM or spleen under steady-
state conditions, indicating that the absence of β2-ARs does not result in abnormal retention in
these tissues, at least in the short term.
Comment-11: Assessment of neutrophil purity after magnetic sorting for proteomics studies is
missing
Response: Before subjecting neutrophils to any downstream applications, including
proteomics, we always conduct a quick flow cytometry analysis to confirm their purity. This data
has now been included in the proteomics figure 3B.
Comment-12: Full list of differentially abundant proteins to provide as supplementary table,
here only unannotated heatmap + pathway analyses are shown. It would be a good addition to
provide some cross-validation of proteomics and flow cytometry data e.g. do the authors see
downregulation of CD62L in the proteomics data and can some up/down proteins identified by
proteomics be validated by flow?
Response-12: We have included the complete list of proteins identified in our proteomics
analysis in the supplementary table; please refer to Sheet 1 labeled “Proteins” for relative
abundance data. CD62L was not detected, likely due to its well-documented shedding upon
neutrophil activation following MI. As a surface protein, CD62L is rapidly cleaved and released
into the extracellular space, and since our proteomics analysis was performed on cell pellets—
which exclude shed or secreted proteins—it was likely not captured. Similarly, several other
surface proteins were also absent from our dataset for this reason.
Comment-13: -Lines 307-308: ‘Administration of NE resulted in the activation of an immune
response that was very similar to that induced by MI’ : how was this formally quantified?
Overlap of up/down proteins induced by MI or NE?
Response-13: This conclusion was based on the observation that both MI and NE similarly
influenced pathways related to immune cell movement and trafficking, with comparable pathway
activation scores (MI: 22.6; NE: 24.7). However, we acknowledge that the original wording may
6
have overstated the similarity. We have revised the sentence to more accurately reflect the data
and clarify that while there is a comparable impact on specific pathways, we did not formally
quantify the overlap of individual upregulated or downregulated proteins between the MI and NE
groups.
Reviewer #3
Comment -1: A major limitation of the study is the use of the permanent ligation of the LAD to
induce myocardial infarction in mice, a species devoid of collateral coronary circulation (which in
contrast is abundantly present in the canine model). Full LAD ligation will prevent influx of
inflammatory cells (neutrophils and monocytes) in the infarcted area in the first few hours after
ligation, despite the statements to the contrary by the authors. They do not provide any
histological data at 6h post MI that would corroborate the presumed influx of neutrophils in the
infarct territory. The FACS data, listed in figure 1 to underpin their claim, do not provide the
required scientific evidence to substantiate this critical statement, as the data are derived from
whole LV homogenates. The authors need to provide histological sections prepared at 6h post
MI and stain for the presence of infiltrating neutrophils. They should next (semi)quantitate the
degree of trafficking in their subsequent studies with different pharmacological and genetic
interventions.
Response-1: We recognize that the LAD ligation model does not fully replicate the clinical
presentation of human acute coronary syndrome (ACS). However, our study design was
informed by recently published guidelines for in vivo murine models of myocardial infarction
(PMID: 34623181; PMID: 34114891), which provide standardized recommendations for both
reperfused and non-reperfused MI models. These guidelines outline key benchmarks for
evaluating left ventricular (LV) remodeling and function post-MI and support the use of the non-
reperfused LAD ligation model as the preferred approach for mechanistic studies of post-MI
inflammation.
To further address this limitation, we performed additional studies using an ischemia-
reperfusion injury (IRI) model to assess early neutrophil infiltration into the heart at 6 hours post-
injury. We also investigated the effects of short-term β-adrenergic blockade with propranolol on
neutrophil recruitment, and evaluated cardiac structure, function, and injury using cardiac
troponin I (cTnI) as a biomarker. These additional findings are now presented in Supplemental
Figure S7.
Regarding neutrophil influx during coronary ligation, it is important to note that neutrophils retain
the ability to access injured cardiac tissue even in the absence of reperfusion (i.e., during
occlusion). These cells can traverse the vascular endothelium in a luminal-to-abluminal direction
to reach the site of injury and contribute to systemic inflammation. This migratory behavior has
been elegantly demonstrated using 4D imaging by the Nourshargh group (PMID: 21706006)
and in vivo imaging by Paul Kubes (PMID: 28983053).
To confirm neutrophil presence in infarcted tissue in our model, we performed
immunohistochemical staining of ischemic WT hearts at 6 hours post-MI and observed robust
neutrophil infiltration, indicated by the presence of multilobulated nuclei (Figure R6). These
findings support the suitability of the LAD ligation model for studying early neutrophil responses
following myocardial injury.
tissue, it is important to emphasize that neutrophils are not cardiac-resident cells like
macrophages; they are recruited only in response to injury (PMID: 31941367). Therefore, the
number of neutrophils remains consistent whether quantified using only infarcted tissue or the
entire ventricle. Flow cytometry, as the most widely accepted method for neutrophil
quantification in the heart, supports this approach (PMID: 28158426, 26358260, 36034743).
Comment -2. The cited references #32, 44, and 50 are not well poised to back up the
statement that “ischemic damage caused by both permanent ligation and reperfusion injury
attracts neutrophils to the infarct”. None of these studies provides histological data on neutrophil
cell infiltration in the myocardium. Moreover, the 37-year-old study by Chatelain et al (ref 50) was performed using a canine model of both ligation and temporary (3h) occlusion and showed
significantly less radiolabeled neutrophils in the infarct region following full ligation (even in a
species with abundant coronary collaterals). Therefore, the limitation reported by the authors
that more temporal studies focusing on earlier time points than 6hrs are required, is not
convincing. To the contrary, additional studies using an ischemia reperfusion model are
indispensable, as well as a larger number of animals per group to increase the power of the
study (at least 10 animals per group rather than 4-6 as is).
Response-2: We acknowledge that some of our initial experiments were underpowered. To
address this limitation, we repeated several key studies, particularly those with fewer than six
mice per group, to strengthen the statistical rigor of our findings. Please see new figures 5L, 5M,
6K, 6J, S1H, S1I, S5H and S5J. Additionally, we now include new immunohistochemical (IHC)
data demonstrating neutrophil infiltration in both reperfused and non-reperfused models at 6
hours post-ischemia (Figure R6). Interestingly, we observed greater neutrophil accumulation in
the infarcted tissue during ischemic-reperfusion injury (50-minute ligation followed by 6-hour
reperfusion) compared to that of permanently ligated MI model, highlighting differences in the
early inflammatory response between these two injury types (Figure R7 and Figure S7).
Comment -3. The histological data presented in figure 5 are very limited and do not allow
proper evaluation of the extent of fibrotic remodeling of the infarcted LV, especially at 30 days
post ligation. One would expect to see full transmural infarction over a large part of the LV free
wall in WT (as suggested by the echo image Fig 5, panel I and as explicitly highlighted in
reference 44).
Response-3: We would like to clarify that we are referring to the extent of transmural infarction.
As shown in Figure 5J (Masson’s Trichrome), the infarct is extensive, encompassing the entire
ventricular wall downstream of the ligation in WT+ MI mice. This observation is further
corroborated by the echocardiographic data, as recommended by the reviewer.
Comment -4. Also, mortality rates are extremely high with only 1 or 2 mice surviving at the 30
day follow up time point. Such high fatality rates do not instill confidence in the experimental
approach when studying novel strategies to regulate what the authors call “runaway
inflammatory responses”.
Response-4: This is partly due to the larger-than-usual infarct size (>30%) induced during
ligation. While we initially started with more than 10 mice per group, the combined effects of
BMT and MI led to significant mortality rates, ranging from 70% in WT mice to 30% in β2 AR KO
mice. High mortality rates are commonly observed in permanent ligation models, and our
findings are consistent with these expected outcomes.
shedding and cell softening is not novel and the finding that MI is capable of inducing a similar
phenomenon is of interest and points toward potential pharmacological interventions to interfere
with this early demargination. Unfortunately, the methodological limitations and lack of outcome
data using beta2-AR blockers do not allow to address our knowledge gaps.
Response: We agree with the reviewer and do not claim that the mechanisms of DEX/NE-
induced demargination (via CD62L shedding or cell softening) are novel. Our experiments were
primarily aimed at identifying a potential target for regulating initial neutrophil recruitment to
prevent the amplification of granulopoiesis, as we recently reported (PMID: 31941367,
34788059). We used butaxamine, a specific β2 blocker, to investigate its effects on neutrophil
demargination and recruitment in mouse models. Additionally, we included propranolol to
assess the translational relevance of our findings to humans, as propranolol and carvedilol are
commonly used in clinical settings post-MI.
Comment-6. The authors report that bone marrow transfer experiments with myeloid cell-
specific ablation of beta 1 and beta1 and beta2 receptors impact on the trafficking to the
infarcted myocardium at 6hrs post ligation (again no convincing data given the methodological
limitations and absence of neutrophil-specific immunohistochemistry) but fail to impact on
survival (staggering mortality rates – see above #4.) or on functional echo parameters.
Unfortunately, more robust MRI imaging data allowing comprehensive function structure
analysis are not available but have become the contemporary standard.
Response-6: We would have delved deeper into characterizing the histological and functional
data if we had identified greater relevance for these studies. The primary objective of these
experiments was to emphasize that long-term depletion of neutrophils, achieved by deleting β1,
β2, or both, is detrimental to cardiac health. These findings align with those observed in studies
involving long-term neutrophil depletion using antibodies (PMID: 28158426) or blocking
neutrophil-derived proteins, such as S100A8/A9 (PMID: 31292614).
Comment-7. The major translational value from this study is the potential role of short-term
inhibition of beta receptor blockade (combined beta1-2 versus selective beta2) on neutrophil
trafficking and subsequent infarct functional and structural remodeling. As presented in figure 6,
it is unclear to this reviewer exactly how many animals were incorporated in the respective
study groups. Again, survival data in the control group do not instill great confidence in the
model and major state of the art diagnostic criteria to evaluate early ischemic burden are
lacking.
Response-7: We initially started with 10 mice per group, but some groups experienced
substantial mortality, with rates as high as 70% in the vehicle-treated group. It is important to
note that these are non-reperfused models, where a mortality rate of 70% in untreated mice is
considered typical. However, short-term treatment with propranolol significantly improved
survival, increasing it to 90%.
Comment-8. The authors should definitely integrate troponin injury markers in their study to
provide more convincing evidence of cardioprotection and rescue of myocardial viable tissue
despite full ligation of nutrient blood supply. In the absence of these corroborating data and
confirmation in a reperfusion model, the data reported here are too preliminary.
Response: Thank you for this suggestion. In response, we conducted additional studies using
both myocardial infarction (MI) and ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) models to evaluate cardiac
troponin I levels at various time points following myocardial injury. These data provide a
quantitative assessment of myocardial injury and allow us to further examine the impact of
short-term (ST) propranolol treatment on cardiac injury, structure, and function. The results
have now been incorporated into the revised manuscript and are presented in Figure S6.

Response: We have substantially shortened the manuscript, particularly the Discussion section
